I run Coached, the behavioral science lab, and Resume Worded, the best software for job seekers. A good place to start is our free 3âminute, science-backed personality test.  Insider trading is illegal in the stock market for a simple reason: it works too well. If you know the drug trial failed before the announcement does, you can't lose. So itâs banned, and people go to prison for it.   But there's a version of it thatâs legal.   Iâll use an example to illustrate first. Take Nokia, the biggest mobile phone company in the â90s. When the iPhone came out in 2007, Nokia's engineers internally knew their phones couldn't compete with the iPhone - their software and hardware were years behind.   The outside world had no idea. To analysts and headlines, Nokia was still the giant of the industry and the iPhone was just a new entrant. But the people working at Nokia really knew how bad the situation was. In other words, they were holding exactly what an insider trader holds: information the market doesn't have yet (that âNokia is screwed!â).   A few of them âtradedâ on it. They retrained, and moved to Apple and Google while Nokia on a resume still opened doors. Instead of trading money, they âtradedâ their careers. But the mechanics are the same - they knew something early because they were internal employees, and used it to do something about their careers.   Most did nothing. They waited for the information to become public and when Nokia's phone business was gone by 2013, everyone hit the job market at once - which was way harder.   My point is: If youâre working at a company, you probably know more about the state of your company, your industry, and yourself than other people. But are you using that information?   Lemme give you three situations where people hold an edge and sit on it:  Things are bad, but you donât act because of comfort: This is the Nokia situation. The product hasnât really improved, or itâs being eaten by AI, the best people are leaving, and there are constant reshuffles. This is useful info: youâre seeing issues before management decides layoffs are necessary. In software, it often looks like the roadmap being rewritten every quarter, the engineers who built the core system quietly leaving, or a migration thatâs been ânearly doneâ for two years. âUsing itâ is getting closer to the faster-growing competitors, or building new skills - like the people who left Nokia early.  Move closer to the âgoodâ. Say thereâs an initiative at your company thatâs doing very well. Thatâs inside information too. âUsing itâ means getting closer to that good, before it becomes the official center of the company and gets super competitive. In tech, that might be the internal platform other teams keep asking to use, or the small AI project whose usage keeps climbing before anyoneâs announced it.  If youâre job searching: Most people apply to jobs based on big brand names, even though they arenât necessarily the best companies. Use your own experience to build your search around where the opportunities are.   Almost everyone has that gap between what they know and what they're doing about it - itâs normal! I want to dig into why.   We donât act on stuff like this because weâre often waiting for one of three confirmations: the numbers to show it, someone official to say it, or the move to finally feel justified.  The numbers arrive late. This is why most of Nokiaâs engineers didnât leave even though the writing was on the wall. Nokia had a record year in 2007, the year the iPhone came out. It just took time for the numbers to catch up. The cracks you see now show up in 3-4 years.  People wait for confirmation, and confirmation never comes. Researchers who studied Nokia's collapse found that middle managers were afraid to pass bad news upward. Execs had a reputation for shooting messengers, so at every layer of the company, reports got a little more optimistic. "We're in serious trouble" left the engineering floor and arrived at the top as "we're on track."  And the feeling of "now it's justified" comes last. Think about what "justified" actually means â it means the situation has become obvious enough that anyone would agree with you. But at that point it's not âinside informationâ anymore because everyone knows it. The edge was when the move was still a bit early.   If you're unsure what you know, here are a few things you can run that no outsider can.  Customer energy: Do customers still love the product the same way, or have things changed?  Pivot speed: When something clearly isn't working, does it get killed in a quarter, or does it limp along for two years? This tells you how fast your company admits mistakes â and companies that admit mistakes fast handle big shifts (like AI) much better.  And the big one right now: AI. Every company is currently figuring out how much of its work AI changes â and the official story about how that's going is the most delayed, most softened information in the building, for all the reasons above. Your inside view is far better.   Check whether leadership personally uses AI â not sponsors it, actually uses it, on their own work. It's hard to make good decisions about something you've never touched (imagine a CEO setting mobile strategy in 2008 who had never held a smartphone). If youâre an engineer, the quick version: are the people mandating AI coding tools actually using them on real work, or just announcing them?   You can also see how AI is landing on your own role: which parts of your job it's already doing, which parts it can't touch. For a fast, structured read on that, get your AI impact map â enter your LinkedIn, and it maps where AI is landing in your specific role.   Get your AI impact map   Itâs free (for now, not forever!).   One honest caveat: insiders get it wrong too. Plenty of smart people were sure Nokiaâs next phone would turn things around, and in hindsight everything looks more obvious than it felt at the time. Thatâs why the trade doesnât need to be dramatic.   Career trades are usually small. If things feel bad internally, the trade is spending your learning hours on the skill you'd need at your next role, and taking the occasional recruiter call while you still have a job.   If something's working, the trade is getting closer to it now â a coffee with someone on that team, volunteering for a piece of it â before it becomes official and everyone wants in.   If you're job searching, the trade is aiming your search at the corner of your industry you know is growing, instead of the famous names everyone else applies to.  Sometimes the trade is realizing you're in a good spot. Many companies pass these checks fine â the product's improving, good people keep joining, bad projects get killed. If that's what you find, great: you can ignore the scary layoff headlines about your industry, because you have better information about your own employer than any journalist does.   This is Coached Weekly, my career notes where I share the tiny % of ideas that actually work in real careers. It takes 5 minutes to read, but could speed up your career by years. âRohan Mahtani (LinkedIn) Subscribe on Coached â âWhy smart people miss whatâs comingâ looks at the same blind spot from the other side: dismissing what a new tool is becoming. A new financial filing provides fresh details — and more questions — about a mysterious $975 million deal struck by TikTok's top star, Khaby Lame. On January 9, Lame — who has over 160 million followers — entered into an agreement that would theoretically net him a major payday and take his company public. The mechanism: a merger with the publicly traded Rich Sparkle Holdings, a financial printing firm based in Hong Kong. Then, in late January, Lame went silent on the merger. Now, we have an update: the deal is still on ice. A Rich Sparkle financial filing on September 30, its first since March, described the deal as conditional on a due diligence process, a minimum valuation of Lame's company, and stock exchange approval. That's the same language that has appeared in previous filings. While the deal has been in limbo, Rich Sparkle's stock has plummeted 99% from its peak. In the wake of the announcement of the deal with Lame's company in January, the stock shot up to a high of about $180. On Thursday, it closed at $1.93. Several prominent brokerages had restricted or blocked trading in the stock, Business Insider exclusively reported in April. The original deal announcement was celebrated throughout the creator economy, since such rich valuations are rare among influencer-founded companies, and it would give everyday investors an unusual opportunity to directly bet on a creator. The high profile of Lame, a Senegalese-Italian creator who rose to fame from dialogue-free comedy videos, means the outcome of the deal could impact how investors assess the viability of backing businesses centered on individual creators. The January deal terms promised Lame's company 75 million shares, which would be worth about $145 million at Thursday's closing share price. The initial agreement had valued that stake at $975 million. Rich Sparkle and Lame did not respond to multiple requests for comment. At the time of the original announcement, Rich Sparkle said that it planned to create an AI avatar of Lame to do brand deals and sell products on social media. It projected this business could drive more than $4 billion in annual product sales. The new filing contains another intriguing detail: Rich Sparkle issued nearly $39 million in stock to its staff as part of their compensation during the six months ended March 31, resulting in an operating loss of almost $40 million. Demand for the iPhone Duo has been "nothing short of extraordinary," Apple said in a statement to the Financial Times. The company also said it is "working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible." Pre-orders for the ‌iPhone Duo‌ opened this morning at 5 a.m. Pacific Time, and it didn't take long for available stock to dwindle. Within minutes, delivery dates slipped from October 23 to November, and by 5:30 a.m., delivery estimates reached January 25. It is no longer possible to order an ‌iPhone Duo‌ for delivery in 2026 from Apple, and customers who purchase now will be waiting until early 2027. Prior to pre-orders launching, rumors said supplies could be constrained due to manufacturing difficulties. With past iPhone launches where supplies were limited, Apple has sometimes been able to ship devices sooner than expected, so it's possible the company will work through its backlog ahead of schedule. There are no guarantees, though, and it's clear many will be waiting for months. Apple has not yet said whether there will be ‌iPhone Duo‌ stock available for walk-in purchases on October 23, but if there is, we could see long lines outside Apple retail stores for the first time in several years. Apple's website suggests there could be some stock available for store pickup as soon as next week, as there is a note to check back on October 24 for availability. In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details. For the past few weeks, several reports from IDC and Counterpoint Research have been mapping out the impact of rising memory costs on smartphone sales. And while the numbers may vary slightly, it is increasingly clear that Apple has been able to weather the downturn better than its competitors. This week, Pu and Huang released a new investor note reinforcing that trend, projecting that Apple will gain significant market share in 2026 as most of its major competitors see shipments decline. According to the report, Apple is on track to close out 2026 as the only major smartphone manufacturer to increase shipments, with a projected 4% year-over-year gain to 257 million units. That would keep Apple ahead of Samsung, which is expected to ship 241 million smartphones, essentially unchanged from 2025. Apple also topped the rankings in 2024 and 2025. Apple’s share of global smartphone shipments is also projected to climb to 24% in 2026, compared to 20% in 2025 and 19% in 2024. Market-wide, the report projects a 14.2% drop in total shipments to 1.08 billion shipped smartphones for 2026, and further pegs 2026-2027 as “one of the most challenging periods for the industry, driven primarily by sharply higher memory prices, which have already pushed OEMs to reduce shipments and raise device prices.” Back to Apple, the report reiterates that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have received a relatively lukewarm reception, which the analysts partly attribute to competition from the iPhone Duo and criticism of their weight. The analysts also cite production constraints affecting both the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup: Due to hinge constraints, we are reducing the iPhone Duo EMS build plan from 7m to 6m units in 2026. We also lower the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max build plan to 72m units given the constraints associated with the adjustable‑aperture camera. The iPhone Duo went up for pre-order earlier today and is already showing delivery estimates stretching into late January in the US and even further in other countries. With all of that in mind, the report maintained its “Hold” rating on Apple stock, with a price target of $369. Apple shares closed at $343.46, up 0.43% on the day, making it the only major tech stock to finish in the green amid the ongoing sector-wide sell-off. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. With Konami releasing its financial statement today, the company used the opportunity to provide its thoughts on the topic. Itâs possible that investor excitement for the technology would make the company feel obligated to address the seismic shifts the industry is facing due to AI, as well as any potential use cases it may have for Konami itself, in its latest the financial report. Notably, the statement focuses on the idea that, no matter the advancements in AI or its capabilities, certain things integral to game development canât be replaced by technology. âGenerally, itâs thought that AI will allow anyone to easily make games, thus lowering the barrier to entry,â says Hideki Hayakawa, representative director and president at Konami Digital Entertainment. âHowever, I do not believe the market will shift significantly. Barriers to entry have already been lowered by the growth of general-purpose game engines and the growth of user-generated content in games. Also, even if using AI leads to greater efficiency, I believe the most important factor in developing interesting and innovative games is people, specifically creators. Not only that, creators form âteamsâ to develop games, and within that, people from diverse backgrounds exchange and bring together ideas to create never-before-seen new games that expand the potential of gaming. This kind of interaction cannot be replaced easily.â While this doesnât entirely rule out the company using AI, as the report notes at the same time that the technology presents a ânotable opportunityâ and could support developers in some ways, Konami remains cautious in researching it while slowly providing guidance to its teams on guardrails and protocols for whether it is to be used. The statement also mirrors that of other studios like Sega, though Konami emphasizes the idea of players and developers coming together in order to have the most fun with a gaming experience, which an AI experience catered solely to the person making it, no matter its quality, cannot offer. Apple's iPhone Duo Case uses adhesive to attach to the device, according to people who have picked one up. The case comes in two pieces and uses adhesive strips along the inside edges to attach securely to an ‌iPhone Duo‌. An included insert instructs users to peel off the adhesive's protective film, put each half on the Duo, and then press down to make sure it's well-adhered. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ Case is made from polycarbonate and comes in Sand and Navy Blue. It is designed to protect the back of the iPhone where the camera bump is located and the front around the outer display. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned of a potential "shock" to the U.S. economy delivered by a rise in artificial intelligence spending, pledging to contain price increases as a flood of private sector funds drives up demand. "If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognize this as a shock," Warsh said in Bangkok, Thailand, at a conference organized by the International Monetary Fund. A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters. In theory, an onrush of investment in activities like chip manufacturing and data center construction could put upward pressure in general on consumer prices, unless the demand is offset by a new supply of goods and services. "It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s hitting the supply side of the economy," Warsh said. Warsh, who took the helm of the Fed in May, has previously weighed in on the potential impact of AI on the labor market and wider economy. On Friday, Warsh reiterated his optimism about AI, saying the technology would ultimately generate added productivity and wealth. But, Warsh added, "the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one." "We really don’t know what the market structure will be of these new technologies," Warsh said. "Who's going to be making the money?" Warsh acknowledged other shocks faced by the U.S. economy, including "shocks of war and military conflict." The outbreak of the Iran war in February imposed a historic oil supply shock and caused an acceleration of price increases in many countries. A U.S. government report issued this week showed inflation had climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Middle East conflict continued to drive up gasoline prices. Prices rose 3.7% in September, according to new data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Fed's target rate of 2%. "It’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said on Friday. He later added: "I’ve heard resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability. I’ve certainly delivered that resolve." Price hikes prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point in September, marking the central bank's first rate increase since 2023. An increase to the benchmark interest rate aims to slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months. The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections. Consistent with his approach in previous public appearances, Warsh opted against issuing a forecast about what the central bank may do at its meeting later this month. "I don’t pre-judge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have over the balance of this year," Warsh said. Many investors appeared to interpret Warsh's posture as a sign the Fed may hold interest rates steady later this month. Copied to clipboard For Hunter Taylor, the story of Mabē goes back “to the very beginning of time.” In other words, it starts in fourth grade when he met Allie Taylor for the first time.  “I was always in love with Allie,” he tells Entrepreneur. “I just knew that she was my soulmate, that we could do anything together that we put our minds to — I felt like we could tackle the world together.” The childhood sweethearts got married and, in 2022, became first-time parents. They quickly found a glaring gap in the market for baby carriers.  Allie was the first to notice the problem. She had trouble finding a carrier that was both functional and fashionable at an accessible price point.  She mentioned it to Hunter several times, and he finally went looking for baby carriers himself. He quickly found that there was a gap in the market in terms of price point, aesthetics and messaging components. He also couldn’t find a product that checked all three boxes.  “I just remember in that moment feeling so convicted that we were the right people to do this,” Hunter says. By early 2023, the two agreed that they wanted to create a premium baby carrier. Allie also saw an opportunity to reshape the conversation around what it meant to be a new mom. They decided to call their brand Mabē (pronounced maybe), and their brand name and logo are inspired by the monarch butterfly.  “Our mission is simple: Provide a baby carrier that looks and feels incredible,” Allie wrote in a September 2023 Instagram post. “One that empowers you to continue doing everything you love, so you can keep chasing your dreams (whatever they mabē) with your hands free, and your baby in tow.” Her desire to start the brand was also personal: She tells Entrepreneur she remembers feeling “really overwhelmed” as a new mom.  “I felt like everyone was just telling me that I’m gonna lose myself now that I’m a mom,” Allie says. “I was determined to write a different story, and I wanted to continue being who I was as a person in addition to being a mom.” Allie says that carrying her baby in a carrier was “the ticket” or the “unlock” for her to have the confidence to do the things she used to do. Instead of having to worry about carrying around a car seat or a stroller, she could simply carry her baby on her chest.  “The confidence that I had from wearing my baby on my chest was just unmatched,” she says. “However, the carrier that I had was just not the cutest thing. As a new mom, you already are not always feeling your very best. Then you layer on ugly baby gear, and it doesn’t help you feel better about yourself.” The Taylors believed in the product — enough so that they invested hundreds of thousands in personal savings to bootstrap the brand.  To start, they identified manufacturers already experienced in making baby carriers. From there, they went through a months-long sampling process, testing fabrics, adjusting design details and rejecting early versions. “The first one we got was terrible,” Hunter says. They continued working with manufacturers until they felt they had a version worth taking to market. The process moved relatively quickly: They came up with the idea in March 2023 and launched in November of that same year. The brand’s signature Monarch Carrier is designed to look more like a stylish accessory than utilitarian baby gear and is priced at around $129.  The product was central, but Mabē’s growth strategy also depended heavily on Allie’s ability to create a brand voice that stood apart from traditional baby-product marketing. She focused on a customer’s identity and aspirations.  “I acted like a big brand from the very beginning, even though it was just me behind my phone doing all of the posting,” she says. In the early days, she tapped people in her hometown and small-business circle for help. A friend helped build the website. Another took the brand’s initial photography. She also built an Instagram account and an email list before launch. Its marketing message was crafted to speak to mothers as individuals rather than as extensions of their babies. Allie says she regularly asks if a piece of content will resonate, help a customer see herself in it and make her feel something. “Instead of saying something along the lines of, ‘Our carrier has three carry positions and is safety certified, and this is the fabric and this is all the different features of it,’” she says, “I’m talking to the mom and saying, ‘Look what you can do when you put this carrier on.’” That could mean a stay-at-home parent moving more easily through the day or an entrepreneur building a side hustle with a baby on her chest. The product benefits still matter, but Allie sees them as secondary to the messaging. “It’s like selling them who they can become and what’s possible if they believe in themselves and if they feel confident,” she says. The messaging gained momentum. At the time of the interview, Mabē had 176,000 Instagram followers. What's old becomes new again, however — a statement that fits almost every industry, from fashion to music and even tech. Clicks Technology, a U.K.-based hardware company with team members who previously worked for BlackBerry and within the BlackBerry space, is leaning into this trend. Growing from its first keyboard case, there are two devices coming this year: the Clicks Power Keyboard, which is now shipping, and the hotly anticipated Clicks Communicator, which should launch in December. "Something was thrown out with the bathwater when we moved to modern smartphones," Jeff Gadway, co-founder of the company (and former marketing director at BlackBerry), explained in a recent interview. His company aims to bring it back — and possibly a little magic to a market that could sorely use some fresh ideas. I saw both devices in prototype form at CES 2026 earlier this year, and in an interview with Gadway, discussed how the company is bringing razzle dazzle back to mobile.      Clicks introduced its first keyboard case for iPhone in 2024, eventually expanding to make cases for select Android phones, too. To say people were excited would be an understatement. "It was like catching lightning in a bottle that first year," Gadway told me during a recent podcast interview. Interestingly, it wasn't just nostalgia-fueled business executives but also younger folks from the digital native generations who were intrigued. Young adults who had never used anything but a touch- or voice-controlled phone loved the concept as much as they are now learning to love vinyl, CDs, and wired earbuds.      The company has since developed the Power Keyboard, a MagSafe enabled keyboard accessory you can use with any MagSafe-enabled phone or case, or any Bluetooth input device, for that matter. The Communicator is an Android phone reminiscent of a BlackBerry Bold that combines a small screen with a miniature QWERTY keyboard. Instead, this version is magnetic, clipping vertically or horizontally onto the back of any MagSafe-enabled phone or phone case and functioning as a power bank with a slide-out keyboard.      It isn't limited to phones: Use it handheld with a tablet or even as a Bluetooth mini keyboard for your smart TV. If you've ever attempted to enter a password into an app using your TV's remote and on the on-screen keyboard, you know how frustrating that experience can be. Gadway says the use cases run the gamut, from students using this in class with their phone instead of bringing a laptop, to CEOs, writers, and musicians being productive on the go.      Taking things a step further, the Clicks Communicator is designed to remind us of the true purpose of a mobile phone: communication. Newer smartphones are designed for content consumption and creation with bigger screens, cameras, processors, and batteries, says Gadway. "What if you could build a phone that was really optimized for communication?" There are two ways you might use the Communicator. The first is as a secondary phone with its own plan or tethered to your primary device. Maybe you have a company-provided phone on which you aren't permitted to download personal apps. The Communicator can be that secondary device to keep in touch with family, access banking and social media apps, play games, and more. The difference between the Communicator and another smartphone is that the smaller, utility-type screen makes this possible, but it's not optimized for going down the rabbit hole of endless scrolling.      The second is as a primary phone, which Gadway told me is how a lot of pre-order customers have said they want to use it. The Communicator sits between a dumbphone, which eliminates access to distracting apps altogether, paring down the experience to bare bones communication, and a full-featured premium smartphone. The Communicator is a full Android 17 device, though, with access to the Google Play Store, a MediaTek Dimensity 8300 processor, a 50MP main camera, and a 24MP front-facing camera. Clicks even upgraded the RAM to 12GB prior to the official launch. It has legacy features you won't find in most modern phones, like a 3.5mm headphone jack and microSD card slot to expand the built-in 256GB storage. The key is in the design: a touchscreen occupying the top three-quarters (4.03 inches, 120Hz) and a bottom keyboard. It's a constant reminder that this isn't a phone to doomscroll TikTok and Instagram or get caught up in mobile games. You can do that. But you won't want to, and that's a good thing.      Other simple features are meant to further encourage focus, like a signal light, similar to the HiLight button in the Google Pixel 11 Pro series phones. Customize it with illuminating colors so you know when an incoming call or message is from your mom, child, spouse, or business partner versus a spam call or an old friend you don't have time to chat with right now. Clicks is working with Niagara to build a custom Android launcher that can curate messages from your favorite apps on the home screen. Triage these apps, Gadway explains, to help prevent you from getting "sucked into side quests." "What we're doing with Niagara," he explains, "is creating a version of this that taps into the hardware of Communicator using the touch-sensitive keyboard to scroll through your messages, and the keys themselves to delete, reply, forward, or mark as unread right from that home screen without ever having to actually go into the app itself. So, it's a much more purposeful home screen experience."      Modern smartphones do more than ever. But there's something inherently missing from the experience. It stems from nostalgia, for those who grew up using phones with keyboards. But there's also value from a usability perspective for a younger generation who never put their hands on one. Gadway says that with the original Keyboard Case, 40-45 percent of buyers had never used a BlackBerry before. "They wanted to reshape their relationship with technology, have some tech that was a little more intentional, a little more purposeful, and that allowed them to get their screen real estate back and have a more satisfying tactile experience."      "Touchscreen smartphones are amazing," Gadway said recently. "They do so many things. And yet they lack some of that tactility and the ability to accomplish certain things from your phone that you wait to do back at your desk." Originally, Clicks was positioned, at least in the minds of those who clamored to get a look at the original case years ago, as a throwback to simpler times. Today, with the latest generation products, it's evident that a physical keyboard is no longer just catering to the BlackBerry faithful. "There is a much bigger audience than we expected," says Gadway. Touchscreens and voice activation aren't going anywhere. Its current license expires November 10, and a full renewal hearing is scheduled for February 18; the conditional permit runs through February 19. At the hearing, Assistant Attorney General Delancey Houston said the Louisiana State Police Gaming Enforcement Division had found information indicating that some shareholders with at least 5% ownership had not completed suitability review. One shareholder had asked to be treated as an institutional investor, but regulators had not decided whether that classification applied. The board attached seven conditions to the extension. DraftKings must provide the required suitability submissions, or file petitions seeking institutional-investor treatment, within 30 days. It also must submit formal responses about its AI use, prediction-market activity, digital offerings to Louisiana residents and other information regulators request within 30 days. Within 30 days, the company must also review and certify that its marketing materials, commercials and digital advertisements comply with responsible-gambling requirements. Other conditions require DraftKings to name a senior representative to handle board communications within seven days and to cooperate with the board’s directives throughout the conditional renewal. Board members questioned DraftKings President of Operations and cofounder Paul Liberman and Chief Responsible Gaming Officer Lori Kalani at the hearing. Much of the discussion concerned a New York Times report alleging that DraftKings used AI to target losing bettors, as well as how it responds when customers show signs of gambling problems. Houston said the investigation was incomplete and that regulators needed more time to examine the allegations. Board Chairman Chris Hebert said news reports do not establish regulatory violations, but the board must assess issues that could affect gaming integrity and consumer protection. DraftKings disputed the allegation about targeting losing customers. Liberman said the company can use customer financial records to determine whether a person is winning or losing, but said it does not use AI to target losing gamblers. He also argued that many customers lose money over time, so identifying customers as losers would not, in the company’s view, make them a useful target group. That is DraftKings’ position, not a finding by Louisiana regulators. Kalani addressed the company’s responsible-gambling practices, including interventions for customers who may need help. The board’s required review of advertising compliance adds a separate check to the ongoing investigation of the AI allegations. Louisiana’s review comes as regulators elsewhere are examining how sportsbooks use AI in marketing and customer targeting. ReadWrite has covered regulatory scrutiny of sportsbook AI marketing; the Louisiana board’s action, however, remains focused on its own investigation and does not establish that the allegations are true. DraftKings must meet the board’s seven-day and 30-day deadlines while operating under the conditional permit. The investigation is still underway, and the next scheduled decision point is the full renewal hearing on February 18, one day before the extension expires. Harvard University delivered its best investment return in five years as its bet on SpaceX boosted its stock portfolio. That comfortably outpaced the benchmark S&P 500's 22.3% total return over the same period. After accounting for taxes, distributions, and gifts, Harvard's endowment grew by $11 billion to nearly $68 billion. Harvard Management Company's stake in Elon Musk's maker of Starship rockets, Starlink satellites, and AI chatbot Grok was worth $2.2 billion at the end of June, per its second-quarter portfolio disclosure. SpaceX was its number-one holding, more than six times more valuable than its second-biggest position, a sub-$350 million stake in Taiwan Semiconductor. Its next-largest positions — each worth over $150 million — were Cerebras, Amazon, Alphabet, and Nvidia. Its 19 holdings at the end of June were together worth about $4.3 billion, more than double the portfolio's $1.8 billion value three months earlier. Harvard said the strong performance of its endowment, which is nearly 400 years old and comprises about 15,000 individual funds, helped it weather the "abrupt termination of federal research grants" by the Trump administration. It's worth noting that 13-F portfolio disclosures are a snapshot of a fund's US stock holdings on a certain date. They don't include foreign-listed stocks, non-stock assets like bonds or real estate, private investments, or stocks sold short. Harvard said that as of June 30, 14% of its endowment was invested in public equities, 29% in hedge funds, 46% in private equity, 4% in real estate, and the balance elsewhere. Anthropic employees believe that AI will make their labor obsolete. Most US workers don't see their jobs that way at all. The AI company published research on Friday that compares surveys with US adults against an internal poll of 1,334 Anthropic employees. Most of the Anthropic staffers said AI will handle at least 80% of their jobs by 2030, while only about 5% of the US workers felt the same. The research, titled "The AI expectations gap," shows the chasm between how the employees at the AI startup feel and how other American adults feel. Anthropic workers are far more optimistic about the progress of AI capabilities, how much it's already saving time, and how fast the economy will grow. The median Anthropic employee said that by the end of 2030, they expect AI to handle 95% of the work of building a new AI model. Peter McCrory, Anthropic's chief economist, wrote on X that the views might help outsiders prepare for more capable AI systems. "We're publishing this research because Anthropic runs roughly a year and a half ahead of the economy on AI adoption, so what happens at Anthropic could be a leading indicator for the broader world," he said. Anthropic's surveys examined how workers already use AI and how they think it will change. "US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree about what AI can do today," the researchers wrote. "However, they disagree about how quickly it will improve, how widely it will be used, and how large the productivity gains measured by time saved will be." There are a few possible explanations for the discrepancies. Anthropic employees have larger budgets for the tools and often get access to unreleased models. MSCI, one of the world's biggest stock index providers, finalized rules proposed in August that could remove shares of leading bitcoin BTC$81,353.01-holding companies Strategy MSTR$136.76·Market Closed and Metaplanet (3350) from its global equity indexes. Under the rules announced Thursday, companies that mostly hold investments rather than running a real business will be deemed ineligible for MSCI's Global Investable Market Indexes. The final list of affected firms is due Nov. 11 and the change takes effect at the close of Nov. 30.  The decision is important because it affects demand for the companies’ shares. Many investors gain exposure to stock markets by placing their money in funds that track an index. When a company is added to the index, those funds must buy its stock. When it is removed, they must sell, whatever the fund managers think of the company.  "The MSCI episode highlights a growing tension between traditional index construction and the rise of companies that treat Bitcoin as a core treasury asset rather than a secondary holding,” decentralized infrastructure network ZEROBASE said on X. “Passive capital has become an important source of demand for these stocks; any sustained reduction in that bid could tighten the equity-issuance window that several of them rely on to fund further purchases."  The risk is biggest for Tysons Corner, Virginia-based Strategy, the largest publicly listed bitcoin holder, with 848,250 BTC worth about $69.67 billion, according to Bitcoin Treasuries. It tends to fund its purchases by selling preferred shares such as STRC and STRK. JPMorgan analysts have estimated that index exclusion could trigger outflows of about $2.8 billion from MSTR stock. The shares closed at $151.29 on Thursday, down about 72% from their record high of $543 in November 2024. Tokyo-based Metplanet, which closed at 277 yen ($1.75) on Friday, peaked at 1,930 yen in June 2025, according to TradingView. Any selling would hit the shares, not bitcoin. The funds would be dumping the stock, which does not necessarily mean Strategy would sell its bitcoin. But weaker demand for the shares could make it harder for these companies to raise the money they use to buy more bitcoin, a strategy they have long pursued to stack up more coins. Strategy's founder, Michael Saylor, has described the company as an operating business with a software arm, and its bitcoin treasury as a distinct business segment. He has rejected comparisons with investment funds. Strategy, originally MicroStrategy, sells business intelligence software to companies including Coca-Cola and Porsche. MSCI already excludes investment funds and similar vehicles. The new rules extend that to companies that look like them. First, MSCI checks whether a company has substantial operating assets, meaning assets tied to a real business. If it fails, the company faces a second test based on five financial ratios covering expenses, cash flow, changes in asset values and reliance on outside financing. A company flagged on four or more of the five is ineligible. To avoid constant churn in the index, MSCI has added buffers. A member is removed only if it fails the screen in each of its two most recent annual filing periods. A company outside the index is blocked from joining if it fails in either of its two most recent periods. In a first test run using May 2026 data, MSCI flagged three companies for possible removal from its ACWI Investable Market Index. They were Strategy, Metaplanet and Yellow Cake, a U.K. uranium investment company.  MSCI is also ending the temporary measures it announced in October 2025 for companies with digital assets making up 50% or more of total assets. Those measures froze increases in the share counts used in the index and put off additions and size-segment moves for those companies. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 In dentistry, as in other areas of business, new client acquisition is a hot-button topic. When a dental practice wants to fill up the schedule or expand a specific service, the instinctive answer is to get more leads. On the surface, having more leads feels like growth, but volume alone doesn’t tell the whole story. If the wrong people are calling or the team is too busy to respond to inquiries and follow up on promising conversations, a practice or business can end up spending more money while missing valuable opportunities. That’s why the real question isn’t just how many leads a practice can generate but how well it attracts the right prospective patients and turns interest into scheduled appointments, accepted treatment and long-term relationships.  To illustrate the difference, consider two dental practices in the same market. Both want to grow and attract new patients, and both are willing to invest in marketing. One invests heavily in new leads, while the other takes a different path. How does each one fare? The dentist at Practice A believes that higher volume leads to growth. When the number of new patients is low, and the patients coming in aren’t accepting treatment, the dentist’s first instinct is to get more leads by increasing ad spend and launching a new-patient discount offer in hopes that the phone will start ringing off the hook. At first, this strategy seems to work. People call the office in droves, and the schedule fills up quickly. However, the team is quickly overwhelmed by the sudden increased volume. They miss more and more incoming calls, forget to check voicemail, return phone calls, respond to online inquiries and essentially stop following up on treatment conversations. As a result, the number of new patient inquiries drops once more, as does the number of scheduled appointments. While initially, the strategy attracted more opportunities, too many of them slipped through the cracks, and volume slowed to a crawl. The dentist at Practice B decides that the best path forward is to focus on improving the new patient experience and creating an acquisition system that attracts the right people and converts more of the opportunities the practice already has. She invests in a marketing campaign to boost lead generation but also understands that can’t be the entire strategy. The priority for Practice B is to attract quality patients who are a strong fit for the services, values and clinical experience the practice provides. She knows that the practice’s website, messaging, online reviews and follow-up process must work together to inspire confidence and prompt prospects to schedule an appointment. The team has a clear process for responding to new patient inquiries on every marketing channel, focusing their conversations on the patients’ needs and guiding them toward an appointment. As part of their daily responsibilities, team members set aside time to return phone calls, reschedule cancellations and follow up on treatment conversations to ensure patients and prospects receive the attention they deserve. In our example, Practice A places all the burden of new patient acquisition on its marketing, while Practice B treats marketing as one part of the acquisition process. Practice A may generate more raw leads, but because the team doesn’t have time to answer inquiries or a system to manage them efficiently, too many of those opportunities get lost in the shuffle. Practice B, on the other hand, converts a higher percentage of opportunities because there’s a process in place to take a prospective patient from interest to appointment to treatment acceptance. Instead of continually generating new leads, Practice B gets more value from the ones it already has. The practice doesn’t rely solely on volume to grow. Instead, the team works on creating a patient experience that helps to attract and retain quality people. The new patient experience begins long before a patient sits in the chair. From the first impression online, a prospective patient is deciding whether the practice is a good fit for their needs.  That decision process continues through the first phone call or message and carries into every additional touchpoint. When that experience feels personal from the start, trust begins to form before the person ever visits the office. Whether you’re a dentist looking for more new patients or an investment consultant seeking to increase assets under management, before investing in more leads, look closely at how you’re handling the ones you already have. Instead, consider strengthening communication, focusing on the new customer experience and creating a disciplined acquisition system to help you convert more of the prospects you currently have. After a long period of dominance by stocks, some investors may look at that 6% yield as a sign that it's time to switch things up and invest more heavily in fixed-income, said Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist for $350 billion wealth manager Hightower. A record $166 billion was poured into money market funds last week, showing that investors are already taking advantage of rising bond yields and lower prices. But Link, a "glass half full" type of investor, still thinks equities have room to run and is where investors will win long-term. A guaranteed 6% or more coupon is still much lower than the S&P 500's inflation-adjusted 7.7% annual average and won't keep pace if inflation continues to rise. It's been a chaotic year for the markets, but the bottom has still not fallen out. Those returns were "not as easy" as they'd been over the previous three years, but when the Atlanta Fed Tracker still projects growth above expectations, she sees optimism continuing to pay off. Cool Hunting®                How a legendary sneaker designer built a low-carbon, zero-drop trail shoe Unless you’re a paddler, you might not know Astral Designs, which only recently began making several trail shoes and is expanding its clothing offerings. The 20+ year-old company began with a fairly radical idea: to produce an entirely PVC-free, phthalate-free life jacket. By 2008, they’d also eliminated the use of neoprene, and by 2021, they were using the bluesign process across their entire supply chain to reduce climate impacts with every step of what they do. Astral moved into footwear because existing water shoes—and now, trail shoes—were antithetical to Astral’s thinking. You’re out in nature, but what you’re wearing (petrochemicals) are harmful to the environment you’re enjoying. That led to the creation of better-gripping paddle shoes that, in founder Philip Curry’s mind, required a similar materials rethink he’d brought to life jackets. Then came the Nosobo, the first outdoor-specific performance shoe with a replaceable midsole (the part of the shoe that wears out quicker than the outsole). It’s not a new idea—the Nike Kobe 8 hit the market in 2012 with a replaceable midsole—but Astral’s Nosobo was the first shoe in the outdoor market to feature the innovation.  Today’s Techyak follows suit, now with a knit upper made entirely from 100% recycled PET. And they’re made without glue, because these bonding agents aren’t environmentally great, and Curry says “water is really brutal on adhesives; that’s always the failure point.” He eventually partnered with a shoemaking legend, Tuan Le, a Vietnamese refugee who broke through with the Reebok Stomper, an aerobics shoe worn by actress Sigourney Weaver in Aliens. Le also invented the Mizuno Wave Rider running shoe, made shoes for NBA stars Stephon Marbury and Vince Carter for the short-lived brand, And1, and since the early 2000s has worked for everyone from UGG to Boggs to Jack & Jones.   Le says he grew up so footwear-obsessed that he used to sleep with a pair of Nike Cortez sneakers instead of a stuffed animal as a kid. “And I named my pet gerbil Nike.” Fast-forward a few decades and NBA legend Kevin Garnett would ditch a Nike endorsement to instead wear And1s designed by Le.  For the Techyak, Le says he riffed off a classic skate shoe silhouette, but pushed himself into a new space as Astral focuses on zero-drop designs that put the foot in a more athletic position. “The toes are open more, more rounded,” he says, noting that too many shoes make it hard to achieve natural, anatomical movement.  Le, also a runner, says that a typical EVA-midsole running shoe is “breaking down from the very first day,” and yet it’s meant to be a shoe’s backbone. Le and Curry wanted the Techyak to have a stronger spine, with better support without being heavy or clunky. It had to be thin enough to keep the Techyak svelte and lightweight.  Any shoe for an athletic person requires some anatomical language. Le says the shoe has to have a visual flex point, where your toes hinge, whether you notice it or not. “From there you need something that explains that the arch support is exactly where you need it, so that’s the story that we need to tell.”  “I’ve been through this process so many times and translated it in languages from Danish to Japanese,” Le says, talking about different clients and brands. “It’s like singing a song. It’s reggae or it’s country music. The words are exactly the same, traction, cushioning, flex, since humans need the same function. But it’s the tune I play with.” Curry dissects another visual component: color. “We start with the viewpoint of a person in the middle of water, so there’s always a water color in our line.” From that perspective, the philosophy expands into soil and plant life. The colors are meant to be organic, but very specifically, inspired by flora.  As for the original red dot on the shoe, Le took inspiration from Astral iconography and the relationship between a rock, the sea and the moon. In some markets, the red was too unusual for some buyers, so Le revised the visuals. The tiny icon will evolve to a lotus flower, which Le takes philosophically. “I’m lucky. When someone is looking to make a career pivot where they don't have to dedicate so much time to their job, it may seem wise to turn away from the corporate world to focus on something smaller. That isn't always the case. For the most part, the days when someone spends 50 years at the same company up until the day that they retire are long gone. Most of those who participate in the working world are going to change their job a few times in the decades they spend in the employment market. Some estimates suggest the average US worker will switch roles at least 12 times in their career. That's a lot of starting over. The reasons that a person may start to look for a new job are many. Sometimes it is as simple as an unfortunate layoff, and other times, they know that they can get paid more to do something similar elsewhere. Not every career change comes from a desire to be more successful, though; there are also instances where somebody still wants to earn an income, but they don't want so much stress.  For those who value a work-life balance above all else, there are sacrifices that must be made at work to achieve that. So long as those sacrifices actually lead to what they want, that isn't so bad. The Exmoor Dark Skies festival celebrates its 10th anniversary in 2026 Stargazers and astronomers are preparing to enjoy a festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky. The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival is being held from 16 October to 1 November and this year is its 10th anniversary. Taking in villages and towns surrounding Exmoor National Park, the event offers walks, talks and shows - putting the dark, clear, night sky into full focus. But what is the event all about - and what is behind its success over the past decade? 'Strong and brave' heritage railway chairman dies Police warn online grooming of children is 'getting easier' Top autumn walks as leaves expected to be more vibrant The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve. Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution. Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it." There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows. Photographers and astronomers can enjoy clear views of the stars during the festival Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting". "In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations.  "You can see the Milky Way - it really is fantastic." Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop. Locations such as Wimbleball Lake are big draws The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season. In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book". The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park. Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down.  "We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend." Americans have a privacy problem, which shouldn’t come as any surprise. Between Ring’s now scrapped interconnected doorbell feature “Search Party,” the unprecedented backlash around Flock cameras, and data brokers quietly selling away our identities, individual privacy is center stage for Americans right now. I would go as far as to make it the inaugural Security Bite ‘Theme of the Year.’ Yet despite all of that, a new survey from data removal service Incogni found that 45% of the 1,517 U.S. adults polled say they aren’t concerned about their online privacy. That wasn’t even the best part of this survey though…  Among people who said they have nothing to hide, 58% would refuse to hand a stranger their unlocked phone for any amount of money, 39% cover the camera on their phone or laptop, and nearly half wouldn’t hand over their text messages to the government or “Big Tech,” even for three months of their income. I asked Ron Zayas, founder and CEO of Ironwall by Incogni, what’s actually going on here, and he basically replied that privacy only feels abstract until it isn’t. “We take privacy for granted, until it means that someone will read our messages, charge us more, put us in danger or disclose intimate details about us,” he told me. “But the reality is, all of that is privacy.” He also thinks companies lean on that gap on purpose, pointing out that if a privacy policy actually said “download this app and we will go through your contacts, suck in your photos, analyze your habits and share those details with anyone willing to pay us,” most of us would pause. Instead, they open with “we value your privacy” and bury the rest in legalese. The survey also found that 65% of respondents have no idea how many websites they’re registered on, and honestly, I’m not sure I could tell you mine either. We’ve all spent the last decade or so creating accounts for things we used once and forgot about, and every one of them is still holding onto something. You can’t protect data you don’t remember giving away, right? So I asked Zayas where someone on an iPhone or Mac should start if they want to cut that down without going full underground, and his answer was more Apple-friendly than I was expecting. “Apple has some pretty good safety protocols, much better than Google in my opinion, and makes them far easier to access,” he said. “Turn off as much of ad personalization, location sharing and contact sharing as you can. It only takes a moment.” He also recommends treating your phone number like you would a credit card number. Allowing an app to have access to your contacts will also give it your own. Zayas put it well when he said that believing you have to “go full bunker in Montana” to have any privacy is a fallacy companies push to make people feel helpless, and I agree with him. If you live in California, the CCPA and Delete Act let you force a good chunk of your data off the market for free. For everyone else, a few minutes to clean things up in Privacy & Security can go a long way. The survey honestly put it better by saying, most of us already act like our privacy matters, so we might as well stop saying it doesn’t. Ron Zayas will join the Security Bite podcast next week. The Information reports that PayPal and Epic Games are among the developers concerned that a potential antitrust settlement between Apple and the DOJ might not go far enough in addressing the company’s allegedly anticompetitive practices. Here are the details. A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple and the DOJ were in talks to settle a 2024 antitrust lawsuit alleging that the company illegally monopolized the US smartphone market at the expense of consumers, developers, and competitors. When the DOJ first filed the lawsuit, Apple pledged to “vigorously” defend itself and has continued to push back against the government’s allegations ever since. Despite Bloomberg’s report about settlement talks, the case has continued to move forward, with Apple and the DOJ recently clashing over access to internal documents from federal agencies during discovery. However, as The Information reported today, settlement talks have also continued behind the scenes, with the Justice Department apparently prioritizing iPhone interoperability. According to the report, the “department appears to be focusing on a deal addressing interoperability issues developers face with the iPhone,” although developers are concerned that any resulting settlement might impose only limited restrictions on Apple’s practices. From the report: As part of its talks with developers, the Justice Department has asked them for a list of ways to improve the iPhone’s ability to operate with other devices, the people said.Many developers and antitrust lawyers are concerned that the Justice Department will oﬀer Apple a settlement that imposes relatively light requirements on how its devices interact with other companies’ devices.” According to The Information, PayPal and Epic Games are among the developers that have directly raised concerns about a potential settlement with DOJ officials. Meanwhile, some people involved in the settlement negotiations reportedly expected a resolution much sooner, although the pending Senate confirmation of Adam Candeub, Trump’s nominee to lead the DOJ’s antitrust division, could be contributing to the delay. The report adds that Apple has changed some of its products and policies since the DOJ brought the lawsuit in 2024, including improving messaging interoperability with Android devices, but is likely to resist more substantial changes to its ecosystem, potentially complicating efforts to reach a settlement. Asked about the discussions, a DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on the specifics, saying only that the department would “continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.” Other companies mentioned in the report, including PayPal and Epic Games, declined to comment, while Apple didn’t respond. by Gary Leff on October 16, 2026  A firm that never bought Boeing stock sued the company for securities fraud over the 737 MAX crashes. It bought recovery rights from funds whose purchases came after both crashes and the grounding.  That company may only have owned stock after the crashes and for about a month. On Thursday, Chief Judge Virginia Kendall in Chicago permanently dismissed the lawsuit.   I’ve written frequently about national treasure Matt Levine’s observation that everything is securities fraud. A public company does something bad. Its stock falls. Lawyers find an earlier statement suggesting the company wasn’t going to do the bad thing. The people who lost money owning the stock become victims, too. Southwest’s Christmas 2022 meltdown wasn’t just about stranding passengers. Investors allegedly weren’t told enough about the technology risks. American Airlines firing Vasu Raja and cutting its earnings outlook brought lawyers looking for shareholders to represent. Boeing’s Alaska Airlines door plug blowout became a case about the company’s earlier safety assurances. Spirit Airlines returning to bankruptcy produced claims that investors had been misled about its financial recovery.  The Valinor funds behind the claims bought Boeing shares on or after June 28, 2019, and held them through and after July 24. Lion Air’s crash had happened in October 2018. Ethiopian Airlines’ crash followed in March 2019. The MAX was already grounded when the shares were purchased.  Problems with the MAX were well known.  The funds alleged that Boeing still misled them about the MAX’s certification, safety, investigation, and expected return to service. They said truthful information would have caused them to avoid buying the stock or pay less.     Buying after a crash doesn’t give a company permission to offer a misleading account of what comes next.  That’s fair enough, although it was always quite clear that the process was uncertain, outside of Boeing’s control (political) and involving regulators around the world. In July 2020, the funds transferred their right to sue to a third party, Value Recapture Partners. The firm filed this suit against Boeing and former CEO Dennis Muilenburg in December 2023. In a letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Value Recapture explained that it buys claims from investment funds that are shutting down. Otherwise, a fund might have to keep operating for years to monitor lawsuits, file paperwork, and distribute whatever eventually comes back. Selling the claim lets investors get some money now and close the fund. The buyer pays for an uncertain future recovery.  But private securities fraud suits have restrictions that buying a claim doesn’t necessarily overcome. The Supreme Court’s Blue Chip Stamps decision limits private damages claims under Rule 10b-5 to actual purchasers or sellers of securities. The Court wanted documented transactions anchoring these cases, rather than lawsuits from people claiming they would’ve invested differently if only they’d been told the truth. Other courts have permitted assignments. In one Chicago case, the original investors retained their claims through a separate company when they sold their investment business. But they were still the people seeking recovery. The judge’s initial February dismissal distinguished that arrangement from selling claims to an unrelated business. She applied the purchaser-or-seller restriction to reject Value Recapture’s standing.  Boeing and Muilenburg had already settled Securities and Exchange Commission proceedings over misleading statements following the crashes, agreeing to pay $200 million and $1 million. Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say. Save Share China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy. The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.     Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government. But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know. China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024. Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold. Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month. The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not. A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt. China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera. The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible. The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said. “I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks. America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold. Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said. The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.      Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.” But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed. “The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially. Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves. China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said. “The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.” Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council. Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024. Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

The very limited supply became painfully apparent when mere hours after launching, Apple’s online store was already showing a shipping date of January 22. For context, Apple is expected to sell a combined 72 million iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max units in total by the end of this year. Enhanced geothermal systems can provide constant, reliable electricity and heat with minimal emissions, but high drilling costs and uncertain cost reductions leave their future unclear. We explore scenarios for the future adoption of these systems in a carbon-neutral, multi-sector European energy system. Here we show that in a net-zero system, heat (co-)generating enhanced geothermal plants at current cost can support 20–30 gigawatts (GW) of thermal capacity in Europe, primarily driven by district heating demands. If drilling costs were to decrease by approximately 60% relative to 2020 costs, the technology would become competitive in electricity markets, greatly expanding its market opportunity. However, the spatially dispersed rollout of district heating stands against the confined overlap of high geological potential with low potential for other renewables, which conditions the competitiveness of electricity-generating plants. This results in a challenge where the majority of the market potential depends on pan-European technology learning for cost reductions, emphasising that coordination is crucial in stakeholders’ efforts. Anker aims to disrupt that space with the Anker Soundcore Space 2 Pro, priced at two hundred dollars. Comfort is a major strength for this headset during long listening sessions. The large earcups feature soft protein leather wrapping plush slow rebound memory foam that was designed using data from over two thousand head profiles.  Weighing approximately 262 grams, the lightweight frame distributes weight evenly across the padded headband without creating clamping pressure. The ear pads can also pop out easily if you ever need to install replacements down the road. For storage, the earcups rotate on a vertical axis and fold in one direction to compact down into a ball. Google Fast Pair simplifies Android setup, while dual device multipoint pairing keeps your phone and laptop connected at the same time. An internal wear detection sensor automatically pauses media playback when you take the headphones off and resumes playback when placed back on your head. The companion Soundcore app expands customization and sound tuning options. Users can take the HearID 5.0 hearing test to generate a custom frequency curve tailored to their personal hearing. An eight band graphic equalizer allows manual sound adjustments across different frequencies. Bonus app features include 3D spatial audio, white noise nap mode, and real time language translation capabilities in over one hundred languages. Call quality is the standout headline feature on the Space 2 Pro. Anker built the headset around its proprietary Thus AI chip and an eight microphone array, utilizing six dedicated voice enhancement mics to filter out ambient noise. It effectively silences office noise, air conditioning hums, and low frequency commuting sounds.  Ambient transparency mode allows clear face to face conversations without removing the headset, though a faint background hiss can be heard when audio is paused. Audio reproduction is driven by 35mm dual material drivers tuned with an energetic V shaped sound profile. The low end delivers deep, punchy bass that brings weight and impact to modern pop, hip hop, movies, and gaming content.  Midrange vocals come through crisp and easy to follow, while sparkling highs provide detailed imaging and a spacious soundstage. Listeners who prefer a flatter response can refine the sound signature using the eight band equalizer inside the app. By pairing world-class AI call clarity with adaptive noise cancellation and plush memory foam comfort, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 Pro bridges the gap between mid-range pricing and true flagship performance Endurance is built for long working days and extended travel. Anker rates the Space 2 Pro for up to 60 hours of playback with active noise cancellation turned off and up to 30 hours with noise cancellation enabled. In real world heavy usage testing with active noise cancellation and high bitrate LDAC streaming, the headset logged over 26 hours of continuous playback. Charging efficiency is fast and practical for busy schedules. A brief five minute charge over USB C provides up to eight hours of listening time. This fast charging capability ensures you can quickly power up before a flight or work shift even if you forgot to charge overnight. Overall, I’ve found the charging and the battery life to be well within Anker’s claims. Pinnacle Selection represents our highest honor, one reserved for products that stand out in design, performance, and overall value. Products earning this distinction exemplify excellence across the board, delivering an experience that truly rises above the rest. When you see the badge, you’re looking at the best of what’s available in its category. The Anker Soundcore Space 2 Pro delivers exceptional overall value at its two hundred dollar price point. By pairing world class microphone clarity with adaptive noise cancellation and plush comfort, Anker successfully bridges the gap between mid range pricing and flagship capabilities. Whether you spend your day jumping between conference calls, commuting on busy public transit, or focusing in an open office environment, the Space 2 Pro offers a complete practical package. It stands out as a highly recommended choice for both brand enthusiasts and budget conscious consumers seeking top tier features.
