The announcement is all upside. Two companies become one, the market likes it, and the integration plan promises a cleaner, cheaper combined operation. Then the work starts, and about six months in, somebody on the infrastructure team is standing in a half-powered data center that no longer has a purpose, wondering who is supposed to decide what happens to all of it. This is the unglamorous back end of every merger. When two organizations combine, they almost always end up with duplicate infrastructure, and a lot of it is physical. Redundant servers, storage arrays, network gear, and the racks they live in. The applications get consolidated onto one platform, the losing site goes quiet, and a large pile of still-working, still-valuable hardware is left behind with no owner and no plan. How that pile gets handled, or ignored, is worth real money and real risk. Here is how it tends to play out, and how to make it go better. In the integration plan, “decommission the legacy data center” is usually one line on a slide. In reality it is hundreds of assets, each of which needs a decision. Some of it is worth redeploying. A lot of it is worth selling. Some of it is only fit for recycling. And nearly all of it holds data that is now the combined company’s problem to protect. The reason this gets underestimated is that it arrives at the worst possible time. The integration team is buried, the people who knew the acquired environment best may already be heading for the door, and the hardware itself is quietly aging out of its best resale window while everyone is busy with the migration. By the time anyone gets to it, the gear is worth less and the knowledge of what it even is has walked out with them. The first real task is working out what you actually have, and that is harder than it sounds after a merger. Each company kept its own asset records, in its own system, with its own naming conventions and its own blind spots. Neither inventory was built to be read by the other side. Merging them is tedious work, but it is the foundation for everything else. You cannot sell, redeploy, or securely retire hardware you cannot see, and you certainly cannot prove later that every data-bearing device was accounted for. A clean, reconciled inventory, with model, configuration, age, and data status for each system, is what moves the rest of the project from guesswork to a plan. Once you can see the full picture, most of the hardware sorts into three paths. A portion is worth keeping, if it matches the surviving company’s standard and has useful life left. A portion is genuinely finished and should be recycled by someone who does it responsibly. And a large middle portion still carries solid secondary-market value. That middle group is where acquirers leave the most money behind, usually by default rather than by decision. Recent servers, storage, and networking equipment can hold significant residual value, but only while they are current. Running that equipment through a structured data center liquidation, instead of letting it sit until it is obsolete, is the difference between recovering a meaningful sum and paying to haul away gear you could have sold. There is one part of this that is not optional. Every drive, array, and system that held data has to be sanitized or destroyed, with documentation to prove it. After a merger this matters more than usual, because you have inherited data from another company, and you may not have full visibility into what is on it or which regulations touch it. A credible disposition partner gives you a documented chain of custody and a certificate of destruction for every data-bearing unit. Those records are not busywork. If a regulator or an auditor later asks how the acquired company’s information was handled during the integration, the paperwork is the only answer that holds up. The single best move is to treat hardware disposition as part of the migration plan, not the cleanup after it. Work backward from the date the legacy site has to be empty. Leave time for inventory, data destruction, physical removal, and transport. Get the equipment valued while it is still racked and running, because operational status is one of the biggest factors in a strong offer. Do that, and the end of the integration looks very different. Instead of a rushed scramble to empty a building before a lease deadline, with aging hardware and nobody left who understands it, you get an orderly handoff that returns money to the combined business and closes the data risk cleanly. When in the integration should we deal with the retired hardware? As early as you can, ideally as part of the migration plan rather than after it. The equipment is worth the most while it is current and running, and the people who understand the acquired environment are most likely to still be around. Who typically owns this in a merger? It usually falls between teams, which is exactly why it stalls. It works best when one person or group is explicitly handed asset disposition, with a deadline tied to when the legacy site must be cleared. What is the biggest financial mistake companies make here? Waiting. Idle hardware loses resale value every month, and a site left running also burns power and space budget. The second biggest is stripping machines for spares that then sit unused, which quietly lowers the resale value of the systems you stripped. How should we handle data from the company we acquired? Treat every data-bearing device as in scope for certified destruction, and keep the certificates and chain-of-custody records. You are now accountable for that data, so documentation matters even for systems you did not originally deploy. Home » Articles » Getty Images Is Going Private Through Bankruptcy. Should Photographers Worry?              Team Lula                  October 16, 2026     4 minutes read Is the biggest name in photo licensing about to take your royalties down with it? Probably not.  But “probably” is worth a look. On October 12, Getty Images announced it’s going private through a prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The Getty family and Koch Equity Development plan to put up to $533 million into the company and own all of it when the dust settles. Getty expects that by the end of the year.  Let’s sort out what it means. This is a reorganization. Getty plans to keep the lights on, fix its debt and keep selling pictures. Getty says it expects “no anticipated impact” on contributors, customers or employees, and that vendors get paid in full like normal. The libraries stay online. That’s Getty’s plan, though, and a court still has to sign off. Photo Business News dug into the restructuring agreement and found it never mentions royalties or gives contributors their own creditor class.  So file “no impact” under hopeful forecast. One more thing, since we’ve already seen folks mix this up. Getty Images is a licensing company. It’s separate from the Getty Museum and the J. Paul Getty Trust. It’s been a rough couple of years. The timeline:  Under the plan, $270 million in unsecured notes disappear, secured lenders accept lower interest and more time, and public shareholders get wiped out. Mostly.  But “AI killed Getty” is too easy. On Getty’s August earnings call, CEO Craig Peters pointed to two sore spots. Ad agencies are making more of their own images in house, and AI is part of that.  And search engines now answer image questions with AI summaries, so fewer people click through to iStock. Now the flip side. That same quarter, Getty’s editorial revenue grew 9.2%, thanks to news, sports and archive demand.  Some of that bump came from a change in how subscriptions get counted, but the demand was there.   Getty also gave up a $3.7 billion merger rather than sell Shutterstock’s editorial arm. That tells you where Getty sees its future. So the squeeze hits cheap, self-serve stock hardest. Debt and a busted merger did the rest. If Getty files, royalties you earned before the filing could count as unsecured claims.   Companies in Chapter 11 often ask the court on day one for permission to keep paying key suppliers. Whether contributors make that list is the thing to watch. Getty pays royalties a few months after each statement, so most contributors have a quarter’s worth of money in the pipeline right now. The realistic worst case is that money showing up late. Your portfolio stays yours, and so does your copyright. Here’s a suggested to-do list if you’re working with them: The bigger long-term risk is outside the courtroom. A private owner can change royalty rates.  Keep an eye on yours in 2027. Editorial is the part of Getty that’s working, and the company says it’ll lean harder into news, editorial and archive work. That should be good news for lots of photographers.   Selling prints directly? You’re in the clear. Getty’s trouble is a licensing and balance-sheet story.  Collectors still want great photographs, and a stock agency’s debt changes nothing there. Worry less, pay attention more. A distributor in money trouble doesn’t mean your photographs lost their value.  It means the middle of the market is shifting, and generic stock is feeling it first. Photographs with a point of view, real news coverage and work only you could make are holding up fine. Keep making those. And keep good records. Save Share Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory. He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments. Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily. Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems. Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield. Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus. Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without. Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis. Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea. With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department. Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year. Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital. For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line. “It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said. Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said. Palestinians know Mekorot well. In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements. Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements. “Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said. Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said. At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast. The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace. The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail. Health is the newest. Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters. Israel has also been flexing its military muscle. Israeli special forces have trained in Cyprus’s Troodos mountains, whose terrain resembles southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies. In 2022, the two armies held their largest joint exercise yet, simulating a war with Hezbollah, The Jerusalem Post reported. Cyprus is replacing its Russian-made air defences with the Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, with deliveries beginning in late 2024. Israel presents itself as a guardian against Turkiye. Following a coup in Cyprus backed by Greece’s military government in July 1974, Turkiye invaded the island and has occupied its northern part ever since. Only Turkiye and its Turkish Cypriot leadership recognise Northern Cyprus. In late December 2025, Israeli and Cypriot military officials signed a 2026 cooperation plan covering joint exercises, training, and “strategic military dialogue”, the Israeli military said. As someone who has been lucky enough to have hands-on with many Windows laptops over the years for the purposes of review, I've grown accustomed to the creature comforts that each brand brings to the table for their specific ecosystem. They all have their own specific flair, and recently, when I was reviewing the Lenovo Yoga 9i, I used several of their "Aura Edition" features that Windows doesn't come with stock. This meant things like tapping to pair Bluetooth accessories like the Yoga PC Edition headphones or tapping my phone on the side of the display to quickly share a photo, and in the midst of using these features, I realized that some of the best integrations Windows has at its disposal have nothing to do with Microsoft at all. OEMs are consistently putting forward useful features into their tech and shoehorning them into Windows, when really, it would benefit everyone to have them more closely integrated with the OS. About this article: XDA was sent a sample of the Lenovo Headphone Yoga PC Edition along with the Yoga 9i. The company had no input into the contents of this article An archival compromise, sudo habits and AI fueled attacks reveal trust as the battleground for Linux security. Tap to Pair is one piece of Smart Share, a set of features Lenovo ships on its Aura Edition laptops. You switch it on during Windows setup or in the Smart Share app, and after that, you tap a supported pair of earphones, a headset, or a mouse twice against the left or right edge of the display. A prompt pops up, you confirm it with another double tap or a click, and the accessory is connected. This is a far better connection experience than stock Windows. Tap to Launch does the same thing for phones: press F11 to open Lenovo’s Smart Connect app, tap a paired phone against the edge of the screen, and its gallery opens on the laptop so you can drag photos across. On a laptop that was purpose built for this, it feels tightly integrated. Using Lenovo's Yoga headphones was just as simple and frictionless as opening a new set of AirPods and connecting them to a Mac. Essential maintenance keeps my old Windows 11 system running smoothly. Lenovo isn’t the only one doing this. Samsung’s Galaxy Book laptops ship with Multi Control, which lets a single keyboard and touchpad drive a Galaxy Book, a Galaxy Tab, and a Galaxy phone, along with Quick Share for moving files between them. Asus, HP, Dell, and most other OEMs have these kinds of creature comforts, but they're not all 1:1. They are the kind of thing that differentiates one Windows machine from the one next to it at a big box store, and all of that experimentation and feature competition can be a good thing—it's just not being taken advantage of. Google shows Microsoft how it’s done. The Yoga Pen feels great to use, and the Yoga PC headphones sound excellent thanks to Lenovo's collaboration with Bose, but there have been times when using these accessories that I wished that extra software wasn't required to get the most out of them. Both will pair and be fully functional without Lenovo's software installed, but to get all the bells and whistles like Smart Share and Aura Smart Modes, it needs to be installed and running. Unfortunately, these apps are seen as an opportunity for ad placement and pop-ups about other services like McAfee, which is supremely annoying. Lenovo isn't the worst offender here, and other OEMs are just as culpable for this kind of thing, but if I have your application installed to get more utility out of the other device that has your brand on it, fewer pop-ups about your new mouse would be great. These features are also naturally fragmented, but sometimes this is intentional. Tap to Pair is limited to Aura Edition models and supported accessories, and if you were to buy another set of headphones or a different laptop from a different OEM, you're looking at a completely different set of features. Keep complaining This feature fragmentation is one of the worst things about mixing-and-matching devices in a Windows ecosystem, but Windows does have a track record of providing solutions, just not very quickly.  Swift Pair, introduced in Windows 10 version 1803, shows a connection prompt when a compatible accessory nearby enters pairing mode, which is akin to Tap to Pair. Another example is Cross-Device Resume, which lets you pick up tasks from certain Android phones on your PC. Microsoft has built pieces of this, but when OEMs are building their own pairing systems instead of leaning on what's already there, that's a problem. Microsoft has solved this kind of problem before, specifically with Precision Touchpad, which replaced a patchwork of manufacturer touchpad drivers with an input stack Windows controls. Windows Hello is another good example, and it gave fingerprint readers and IR cameras from every OEM one consistent sign-in experience. In both cases, OEMs already had the hardware, and the experience got better once Windows owned it. Things like Tap to Pair deserve the same treatment. Extend Swift Pair with a tap trigger, let OEMs supply the sensing, and have Windows own the prompt. Accessory makers would implement one standard that works across every brand’s laptops, and better yet, the feature would survive a clean install because it would be part of Windows itself.  Laptops come with too much bloatware, but there are some useful ones. Microsoft’s partners are doing its R&D for free, and they’re absorbing the bloat criticism while they do it. Tapping a pair of headphones against a laptop to connect them is the kind of thing that should make people choose Windows over Linux. Across Sub-Saharan Africa, women workers dominate agriculture but rarely capture the sector’s economic value. With a systematic approach to closing the gap, policymakers, NGOs, and philanthropic organizations could unlock a $1 trillion market and transform the continent’s food systems for the better. WASHINGTON, DC—If you picture a woman working in agriculture in Africa, what image comes to mind? Maybe it’s a young woman with an infant slung on her back, hacking at the soil in searing heat, struggling to find affordable fertilizer or a decent price for her crop. Or maybe she’s a successful entrepreneur building a vibrant food business, employing hundreds of workers, and contributing much to her local economy. While empirical inquiry has its place in economics, the pursuit of causality must not be allowed to displace the pursuit of explanation. Beyond identifying causal effects within existing arrangements, economists must investigate how those arrangements are produced, reproduced, and contested. Both women are real, of course, as are many variations in between. But the fact is that many more women could be leading farming businesses and driving economic growth if the barriers they face were tackled more systematically. With Africa’s food and agriculture market predicted to reach around $1 trillion by 2030, countries that want to harness the most value cannot afford to forgo women’s economic power. In Sub-Saharan Africa, over three-quarters of working women can be found in the agrifood sector, where around two-thirds of their work happens off the farm, in processing, aggregation, storage, and informal trade. Although these are the links in the chain where value is added, the women performing such roles often remain trapped in precarious, low-paid, informal arrangements. At the other end of the spectrum is a growing cadre of dynamic African women food entrepreneurs or “agripreneurs.” I recently encountered some of these women business leaders at the Africa Food Systems Forum in Rwanda, where they were being honored for their success.  Ifeoma Mary Okonkwo, for example, co-founded a solar-powered cassava business in Nigeria that processes 15 tons per day into gluten-free flour, starch, fortified foods, and animal feed for domestic and export markets. In the space of a decade, her company has grown to employ hundreds of people. It has purchased cassava worth more than $4.45 million from its network of 2,000 (mostly women) farmers, while helping them access fertilizer, technical advice, and markets. Okonkwo’s story shows what can happen when governments and donors make a deliberate effort to empower women-led businesses. Among other advantages, she was able to access finance on favorable terms through women-focused lending schemes. A recent World Bank report, Women, Business, and the Law 2026, shows that legal equality on paper does not automatically produce economic opportunity. Women may have the right to register a business or open a line of credit, but their ability to formalize operations, invest, and expand is still limited by weak enforcement, a thin financial infrastructure, restrictive social norms, or unpaid care work. Updating antiquated land ownership laws would be a good start, since inheritance customs and social norms routinely override women’s legal land rights in practice. Still, passing a law isn’t the same as enforcing it, and the same caveat applies to gender-equal business laws. In each case, implementing legal changes matters as much as enacting them. Fortunately, when it comes to empowering rural women to move from subsistence farming to viable small businesses, a growing body of evidence shows what works. In Ethiopia, for example, agriculture employs around 80% of the country’s workforce, yet female farm managers were producing at least one-third less per hectare than men—a gender gap that was costing the country more than $1 billion annually. So, the agriculture ministry, with support from the Gates Foundation, partnered with CARE, an international NGO, on a program that cuts out middlemen by connecting women’s producer groups directly to markets and provides training in climate-conscious farming and nutrition. Over the past decade, this “Farmer Field and Business School” model has expanded across multiple African countries, yielding strong results. In Burundi, for example, women’s crop yields increased substantially. By pooling savings, sharing market intelligence, and lending to one another, women have been able to diversify their small farming businesses, establish credit histories, and build their confidence. India offers a parallel example. PANI, a local organization rooted in Gandhian values, has spread climate-conscious farming knowledge and market access from woman to woman across tens of thousands of households through trained community advisers. Underlying these and other programs is a focus on educating and upskilling women, while addressing the deep-seated gender norms that stifle their opportunities. The Ethiopian project engages men in community dialogues to challenge the norms that treat farming as a male pursuit and household chores as a female domain. The women taking part report greater confidence and decision-making power; both women and men say their partnerships are now stronger as a result. Philanthropy can play its part by helping to scale proven approaches, by backing emerging innovations that are designed around women’s needs—from climate-resilient crops and livestock to AI-powered digital tools—and by linking international financing to clear gender-equality goals. One promising example, a climate-finance model led by the International Fund for Agricultural Development, ties funding to measurable gains in women’s economic opportunities—making gender equality part of the investment itself, rather than a secondary objective. The model has already helped direct $118.5 million in investments in several countries, helping rural women gain greater control over land and productive assets, strengthen their livelihoods, and build resilience to climate change. This last point is crucial, because it is now well established that climate change is hitting women farmers hardest, compounding deep-rooted inequalities. Research in low- and middle-income countries has found that a 1° Celsius rise in average temperatures is associated with a 34% greater reduction in income for female-headed households compared to male-headed households. As the effects of climate change intensify, governments, development partners, and philanthropic organizations must do more to create conditions for rural women to adapt, build resilience, and prosper. Women like Okonkwo show what is possible. They are already sustaining food systems; positioning them to lead will drive the structural changes our societies need. If consoles and GPUs are priced out of reach for years, the market won't simply wait for them to come back – it'll re-centre around the devices people already have Right about now is the moment when the console business should be getting one hell of a second wind. Six years deep into a hardware generation, with probably the most anticipated video game launch of all time just a few weeks out, this should be when the platform holders make hay, extending those mature install bases out into ever-wider audiences as fence-sitters finally pick up the hardware they've been holding out on for years. Instead, even as a flurry of shortages for the seemingly supply-constrained PS5 Pro drives prices up into scalper territory, the overall picture from market data looks genuinely grim. Circana's latest figures show Xbox hardware unit sales for the year through August down 33%, sitting at an all-time low. PlayStation is down 25%, its weakest showing since 2013 – a nadir it reached on the eve of PS4's launch, with the market holding out for the new system. The culprit isn't a mystery. The average PlayStation sold this year has cost a consumer $597; recall that the digital edition of the console cost $399 at launch in 2020. Nobody seems to expect any improvement next year – 2028 is the year when most analysts pin some cautious optimism for a return to a semblance of normality. That's when Circana's Mat Piscatella said he's hoping prices will stabilise, and when S&P Global's forecast suggests that global console sales might start to recover. Demand for games and entertainment won't disappear just because console shipments tank, of course. Even as teeth are gritted and hatches battened down against the market conditions created by the hardware component crisis, it's important to ask where the demand might relocate instead. If consoles have priced themselves out of their target market's acceptable range, where will that market turn for its gaming fix? It certainly won't be to high-end PCs, where the pricing crisis is biting even harder than for consoles. This week brought reports (as yet unconfirmed by Nvidia) that the RTX 5090 graphics card is effectively discontinued, with the company allocating all of its output of GB202 chips to the far more lucrative RTX Pro workstation cards instead. Discontinuation is a technicality for almost everyone; the 5090 has cost more than a small car for the past year anyway, with retail prices north of $5,000 for a card that launched at $1,999. Lower-end cards and even previous generation 40-series cards also routinely command several thousand dollar price tags. Perhaps this starts to sort itself out in 2028; perhaps the situation drags on for several years beyond that. Nobody really knows for sure, so for the sake of argument, let's take the pessimistic case as a premise and see where it leads. Suppose dedicated gaming hardware, both consoles and discrete GPUs alike, is simply priced out of consumers' reach for the next few years, perhaps all the way to the end of the decade. What does that actually do to the games business? I think the answer is actually deceptively simple. If new hardware is prohibitively expensive, the hardware people already own – or the hardware they'll justify buying on non-gaming grounds – becomes the most important platform there is. If you follow that thread of thought, some interesting consequences fall out along the way. The first, and most obvious, is very much in Sony's favour – which I'll grant is an odd thing to say given I just talked about the PlayStation posting a 13-year low in its sales figures. Sony, however, hasn't been making decisions like a company facing a sales crisis and needing to win back consumers – and I think the tenor of that decision-making, and the way it has approached price hikes, may reflect its own understanding that this situation isn't entirely unfavourable for it. Overpriced hardware locks in the PS5's install base advantage. Sony has shipped over 95 million units, and while that number is barely creeping upwards now, it isn't going anywhere either – and there's no prospect of anyone else selling new or aggressively priced hardware that can chip away at that dominance. The same pressures crushing hardware sales will hobble the PS6 when it arrives – nobody is going to enjoy the price tag on a next-gen console with a modern memory configuration – but they also freeze the current market in place, with the PS5 as the dominant home console for as long as that freeze lasts. Sony's business model assumes a reasonably brisk transition to new hardware, and that would probably still be its preference, but unlike Microsoft – which needs a generation transition to give it a fresh roll of the dice – Sony is under no pressure to force one. The company has already decoupled its profits from hardware sell-through; the games division posted record operating income last year alongside falling unit shipments. If a clean generational transition isn't on the cards, Sony will be perfectly content to make hay from several more years of software sales, PlayStation Plus subscriptions, and digital revenue on its existing install base. Microsoft, enjoying no such luxury and trying to turn around a troubled business and brand, will find such a market freeze far harder to cope with. The same logic, though, has consequences that are far less comfortable for Sony, and for consoles in general. If the device you already own is king, then the most widely owned high-performance computer on the planet is the smartphone – and as the most personal and most heavily-used device, it's also the one most likely to get consumers to pay a premium for regular upgrades, even if it's through gritted teeth. Mobile gaming is huge already, of course, but it's largely been seen as somewhat separated from the core gaming market for many years. That isn't guaranteed to remain the case. Games like Fortnite and Genshin Impact already bridge mobile and more traditionally "core" platforms very effectively, and there's been a slow movement building on the fringes of the mobile market to bring more core-style games and business models back to these platforms. The likes of Capcom's Resident Evil ports or Warframe's mobile version haven't transformed the market yet, but a change has been building quietly for a while – and as console and gaming PC hardware hits an affordability wall, the ubiquity of capable phones is going to be increasingly hard to ignore. Hooking a phone up to a TV, pairing a controller, and playing something console-shaped is perfectly possible today, albeit a bit of a faff in many cases; it's only a few usability tweaks and a strong dose of necessity away from being a very normalised way of engaging with games. There's a global dimension to this, too. There are hundreds of millions of players in developing markets who were never going to own a console regardless of price; they've often been low on the priority list for major gaming companies, because revenue per user in those territories is minuscule compared to North America, Europe, or Japan. If players in those wealthy markets are similarly constrained to the hardware in their pockets, though, the whole equation shifts. A game designed for a phone-first audience suddenly has a shot at genuinely global appeal, rather than being a lesser version of something built for a living-room box most of its potential players will never own. Mobile might not be the only beneficiary of the sudden appeal of gaming on hardware you already own. Even if I fully acknowledge that you could fill a library with optimistically incorrect predictions that the stars were finally aligning for gaming on the Mac, it's hard to ignore just how ubiquitous Apple's laptops have become among younger demographics who are also very likely to seek out gaming experiences on their existing hardware. The Mac has always been the bridesmaid, never the bride – largely because Apple itself has fumbled catching the bouquet on every occasion – but the market fundamentals now may be so powerful that even the company's butter fingers can't let the opportunity slip entirely. It's not just that Apple Silicon devices have proliferated massively among students and young people in the past few years (thanks to the very unusual, for Apple, situation of them not only being very good devices, but also very competitively priced). The tooling might be about to catch up, too; a recently released open-source project called NotProton ports parts of Valve's Proton to macOS and switches on the Steam Play functionality that has apparently been sitting dormant in the Mac Steam client, letting Windows games run straight from a Steam library via CrossOver. We've seen what Proton did for Linux gaming and the Steam Deck; if Valve decides to make something like this official – that dormant code suggests it has at least thought about it – it could open the floodgates for Mac gaming at last, with the major benefit that this time it wouldn't even require developers to go out on a limb with the expense and risk of porting games to the Mac directly. Put all of this together and you have a market that, in a few short years, could re-centre itself around a very different set of devices and platforms than the ones we've grown used to. The temptation is always to treat a crisis like this as a temporary interruption to business as usual; a few lean years after which prices normalise, the PS6 and its rivals arrive, and everything resumes its natural course. The longer the situation continues, though, the more consumer behaviours will get accustomed to these alternative platforms, and the less likely a clean regression to the norm becomes. Habits formed over three or four years don't simply evaporate; nor do development pipelines retooled around new target platforms, or players who discover that the phone or laptop they already owned was perfectly good enough. Sony may be able to comfort itself, for now, with knowing that a frozen market is one that freezes in the PS5's dominance. The risk is that if this freeze lasts too long, the landscape that eventually emerges from under the permafrost will have been changed forever. October 16, 2026 3 min read A decade after Theranos imploded, here’s what scientists want you to know A viral documentary has everyone talking about Elizabeth Holmes’s fraudulent blood testing start-up again—but scientists never stopped By Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron Around a decade ago Theranos, one of the buzziest science start-ups ever, imploded. Swamped by allegations of fraud, the actions of the company and its enigmatic CEO, Elizabeth Holmes, shone a harsh light on problems with scientific start-ups. Now scientists say these issues have only gotten worse. In a new documentary titled You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder follows Holmes in the lead-up to starting a prison sentence in May 2023, after she was found guilty of fraud. The film retraces the saga of Theranos, which claimed to have a machine that could perform hundreds of clinical tests using a single drop of blood. After years of fundraising, high-publicity support and partnerships with pharmacies to make the tests accessible, scientists and journalists revealed in 2015 that Theranos’s claims were false: there was no scientific evidence that its product worked. Theranos is, in many ways, a cautionary tale and a relic of 2010s Silicon Valley. But for scientists, Theranos’s problems are anything but history. Canaries in the Coal Mine John Ioannidis is a professor at Stanford University’s medical school and was among the first to question Theranos’s bona fides in a 2015 article. Eleven years later Ioannidis says he worries the problems of transparency and a lack of strong evidence in science and technology start-ups are, if anything, worse today. “I feel kind of uneasy about this being presented as a sensationalist, movie-quality story [about] a single bad apple because I see very similar phenotypes to Theranos,” Ioannidis says. Ioannidis argues that, in some ways, claims of scientific progress are a public relations game. As private companies have become increasingly powerful agents in driving research forward, the trend has shifted fields away from more traditional, publicly funded research and academia. “Holmes is in jail, but the recipe of her success has been even more widely adopted,” he says. Ian Papautsky, a microfluidics researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago, says that Theranos’s public downfall and time in the spotlight create a strong case for validating scientific findings. But he, too, worries that, as start-ups and private companies increasingly drive discovery, opportunities for secrecy or fraud may grow. “Many of the start-ups are not transparent in their technology development,” he says. “On the one hand, you would argue that they have to be, because they’re trying to compete with everyone else. But that also makes it a lot easier to hide the mismanagement and all these other various issues.” Holmes’s husband, Billy Evans, who also appears in the documentary, is himself quietly building a new blood testing company. The start-up, called Haemanthus, plans to use artificial intelligence tools to run diagnostic tests. Holmes is listed as a scientific adviser to the company, and Evans has raised millions of dollars in funding, according to NPR. “The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again,” Evans tells Fielder in the movie. A Lasting Effect Theranos has made it harder for academics who study blood testing or microfluidics to get funding, says Umut Gurkan, a biotechnology researcher at Case Western Reserve University. He creates blood testing products for conditions such as sickle cell anemia. Gurkan remembers going to Silicon Valley in 2015 to seek funding and being told, “We don’t invest in diagnostics anymore.” Even as diagnostic technology has advanced, it remains difficult to bring it into markets, he says. “Trust in science is fragile, and ‘a drop of blood’ now sounds like a scam,” Gurkan says. “Honest companies trying to save lives pay that tax. And at the end of the day, patients and real people pay the price with lack of working diagnostics and technologies that deserve to be in the market.” As for Theranos’s claims: even after more than 10 years of advancement in clinical testing and microfluidics, its premise remains impossible, the researchers consulted for this article say—at least at the scale that Holmes promised. A drop of blood doesn’t hold nearly enough biological information to conduct the hundreds of tests that Theranos claimed. Theranos’s mission was noble, Papautsky says, but the science did not and does not hold up. “Doing multiplex testing on a small volume of blood is a good concept—it would be an important advancement in technology,” he says. “But having experts with the right knowledge and good management is very important, and it’s becoming more and more important these days. Expertise is not necessarily being valued as it used to be.” Mary Randolph is a news intern at Scientific American and is based in New York City. menu 15.10.2026Essay Artificial intelligence is capitalism’s final destination Odilon Redon: The deformed polyp floated on the shores, a sort of smiling and hideous Cyclops (1883) / National Gallery of Art  The auguries are raining down hard. Think or Sink. Comply or Die. Look Up or be Left Out. And so, with these not-so-gentle threats, it has come to pass that the Age of AI – Actual Idiocy, Actual Super Idiocy, Recursive Snowballing-Idiocy – is upon us. Heck, I’ve already used two dashes in this opening paragraph. That, as they say, is a tell. So, perhaps I haven’t written this essay at all. You’d have to use an AI app to check if it’s actually AI, and whether I’m really, or not really, or only partially me. You can no longer use your instincts. You have to use the App. Now that AI owns the em dash, what will future generations make of Emily Dickinson and her love of them? Has she been fed to the machine, too? Will they love her less? Are we being gradually locked out of language? Does it matter anymore? For reasons that have more to do with a writer’s ego than with faith, I have always been enthralled by the first verse of The Gospel According to St John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” I believe this to be true. I believe that disrupting and vitiating the fundamental relationship between humans and language will undermine all semblance of social coherence. AI has crashed into the world of literature, leaving writers, publishers, literary agents, readers, critics, teachers and students feeling the ground give way under their feet. Professors must now look at student assignments with distrust. Publishers have to evaluate new writers like detectives inspecting a potential crime scene. It’s hard to describe what this does to reading or learning. The joy and challenge of intellectual engagement has been replaced by something closed, mordant and mechanical. A taxidermists’ Shangri-La in which everything that was once alive has been skinned and stuffed, and regards you unblinkingly, with a meaningful glint in its bright, spurious eyes. It’s like looking at someone and wondering if it’s really who you think it is. Or looking in the mirror and seeing your likeness, but knowing it isn’t really you. In time, we may forfeit that knowledge, too. Then we will no longer know who we are, or even if we are. And when this happens to a whole society, a whole species, when we can no longer rely on instincts that have been learned over centuries, passed down from generation to generation, when we can no longer trust our hearts, our eyes or our ears, when we can no longer tell truth from falsehood or the virtual from the real, when time collapses and the past, present and future run into each other, when a million languages and cultures are pureed into glop, when an ancient social compact – whatever its limitations and flaws – is smashed beyond recognition, are we setting ourselves up for mass psychosis? This line of thinking may open me to accusations of having fallen prey to the inevitable moral panic that ensues when we’re faced with something new and incomprehensible – the same panic that preceded the Industrial Revolution or the coming of the computer. The question is: is that all it is? Are we just living through an uncomfortable moment of transition in the evolution of human “progress”? Or is this indeed a catastrophic rupture? Perhaps we should listen to the people who are building this glorious new technology. Last month, a young employee at Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, quit his job, saying that his conscience would not allow him to work on a project that could potentially annihilate the human race. The picture he painted of his workplace was more or less the Manhattan Project on steroids. But as we know, this time around the scientists are motivated in large part by profit and a race to “get there first”. What followed Coxon’s resignation was bewildering. The CEOs of the biggest AI companies fell over each other in their rush to discuss, disagree or concur with the whistleblower who had exposed them. Our screens blew up with videos of those billionaire oligarchs informing us in sombre, sepulchral tones that there was a fair chance that the Machine God they are in the process of consecrating could bring about the end of human civilisation. Having established their suzerainty over our species, they reassured us that they were doing their best to mitigate the risk. They made a plea for government regulation. Their cry for help hinted at some sort of pathology. There was something a little kinky about it – a sort of Tie Me Up! Tie Me Down! vibe. Is it that, or is it just the inherent nature of capitalism? Helplessness in the face of untethered greed? The oligarchs do seem to believe in their extinction narrative – at least enough to have built themselves bunkers at the far ends of the Earth stocked with water, food and ammunition. But extinction is not what they are selling the rest of us. (Donald Trump and tech libertarians openly call it a hoax.) Progress, glory and the good of mankind are the marrow of their sales pitch. One of them, Peter Thiel of Palantir, has even gone so far as to call critics and those calling for regulation the “Anti-Christ” who are courting the devil – by default conferring divinity on his company and its aspirations. (Yes, the same person who, when asked whether he believed that the human race should survive, famously replied “Ummm….” and went on to stutter and mumble.) The crackle and pop eventually settled along faultlines that are familiar to tech insiders – doomers, accelerationists, skeptics. But when other voices speak up about the real, calamitous ongoing damage being done by the AI industry, they are deliberately ignored and shut out. Interestingly, the oligarchs seem to be a lot more comfortable with Jacob Coxon than they are with some other whistleblowers. They did not rally in defence of Meredith Whittaker, now president of the Signal Foundation, who resigned from Google in 2019 after she called out its contract to build machine vision technology for US drones. Seven years later, that synthesis between the AI industry and the weapons industry is on display for all of us to see. (Cf. The US double-tap attack on a girls’ school in Minab, southern Iran, in February, in which 156 people including 120 schoolchildren were killed. No apologies were offered, because no one did it. Machine-planned murders come guilt-free. This is also true of Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy?, the AI systems behind Israel’s assassination campaign against Hamas militants in Gaza, in which, according to human rights reports, the basic target unit for the locating and tracking systems was the family home.) There was no outbreak of oligarch support when Timnit Gebru, one of the very few black women in a senior technical role in Silicon Valley, was fired from Google in 2020 for refusing to take down a research paper she had co-authored. The paper exposed the environmental costs of training large language models (LLMs) – including Google’s – and showed how they magnified and reproduced white supremacy and misogyny from the data sets they had swallowed whole. She warned that these pathologies would only be amplified as the models were scaled up and became harder to audit. Her findings were buttressed by another researcher, Abeba Birhane, who co-authored a paper called “On Hate Scaling Laws for Data-Swamps”. Why would Whittaker and Gebru and their very specific indictments worry the oligarchs more than the prophets of all-out extinction like the AI scientist-turned-critic Geoffrey Hinton, or Jacob Coxon? Perhaps because, like a big fireworks display, Hinton and Coxon’s warnings add frisson to the atmospherics. They end up augmenting the oligarchs’ power play, which, when their companies go public, as they are set to do soon, will serve them very well indeed. Their valuations will depend on how sophisticated – and, in the case of AI weapons systems, how lethal – their models are. Who are these billionaires who claim to hold the power of life and death over humanity? They give the impression that they have already disaffiliated themselves from the human race, and from this planet we call home. Are they satyrs? Half-human, half-machine? Let’s call them Cyclopes – “pees”, plural. Those giant, one-eyed, cave-dwelling shepherds from Greek and Roman mythology. (In the twenty-first century, their caves are opulent and their sheep are humans.) Think of them as a single entity. A mutation. Cyclopes has a single head and a single pale, unblinking eye set into its forehead, way to the right of centre, which casts its jaundiced gaze on ordinary humans and sees only what miners see in a mineral-rich forest, or what dam builders see in mighty, flowing rivers. A resource to be extracted, accumulated and put on the market. Fuck the forest. Fuck the river. Fuck the human. But unlike the silent, blundering cyclops we saw on our cinema screens recently, Cyclopes branches at the neck into several squabbling bodies that give the impression they don’t get along, but, when it comes to the End Times – or, more precisely, End Times Fascism, to borrow the title of Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s magnificent new book – they clearly do. Cyclopes’ extinction orgy appeared to many industry watchers as a set piece staged to persuade an increasingly angry, agitated public how central, important, irreducible and un-roll-backable AI companies are to the US economy, and to the security and future of its people. Asking to be regulated is an attempt to graft the industry onto the state, to shut out every last chink of daylight between the government and these corporations. The oligarchs’ hope is that this regulatory embrace will give them the blank cheque they so badly need. Because the scale of money, land, water and energy that they require can only be provided by the government. Not to put too fine a point on it, what they really want is government permission to self-regulate. Legitimacy without ceding control. This sort of delicate manoeuvre needs to be performed like a kabuki play. It needs a villain, a bogey man, to scare an increasingly restless public, and any incoming governments who may not be as malleable as the Trump regime. Enter, stage left, China. To protect the US from the threat of a rising China, Cyclopes offers the US government an array of lethal autonomous weapons systems that other countries cannot dream of, as well as the fantasy of lab-grown viruses and bioweapons thus far unknown to science. To contain and align restive populations domestically, it offers the US and other friendly governments surveillance and facial-recognition systems that promise to make Israel’s Pegasus spyware look like a toy. In return, it demands unimpeded capital flows, and the promise of as much land, water and energy as it needs to service its giant data centres and supercomputers. Translated into direct speech, it goes something like this: we’ll market ourselves as the cutting edge of human enlightenment, and the manager and disburser of human knowledge sans frontières. But in truth, we’ll be map-shaped. We’ll fuse ourselves to our nation, its economy, its intelligence grid and its security apparatus until you won’t be able to tell us apart from yourself. Except for our bank balances. In exchange, you can pretend to regulate us until we achieve our mission to colonise the moon and outer space. No frontiers, no fears. Then we’ll kick away the ladder that you so kindly lent us. We won’t even need to replace you. You simply won’t exist. We will run your people, your cities, your communications, your finance systems, your courts, your army and your police. If not us, it’ll be China that runs you. These pleas by the major US-based AI corporations for government regulation also serve to foreclose competition by smaller players, so that when international treaties on AI are signed (as they must be), it will only be them – the handful of “regulated” corporations – whose hats will be in the ring. The merger between corporations and countries is well on its way. The science of AI may be new. But the way it is being foisted on us is as old as colonialism itself. In India we have a history of being colonised by a company. And yes, our ruling classes invited them in, just as America’s rulers are doing now. The East India Company was eventually taken over by the British Crown. Now, of course, it’s happening in reverse. Much of India’s infrastructure is owned by two corporate conglomerates, the Adani Group and the Reliance Group, both of which are poised to dive into the AI ocean. Cyclopes is readying itself to take over the US state. This is Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir: “I think the central risk to Palantir and America and the world is a regressive way of thinking that is corrupting and corroding our institutions.” He was annoyed by analysts who suggested that Palantir was overvalued. (I mean, how can you presume to “value” a God?) He followed up with some of that trademarked cool, rich-guy type of humour: “I love the idea of getting a drone and having light, fentanyl-laced urine spraying on analysts who’ve tried to screw us.” And this, famously, is Sam Altman, now of Open AI, while acknowledging that AI may be steering humanity on a shortcut to hell: “… but in the meantime there will be great companies created with serious machine learning”. Or how about this, from Marc Andreessen – the uber-accelerationist who is uber-aligned with Trump, and seems to have the same uber-IQ? “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man… We are not victims; we are conquerors.” There are several brands of the Apocalypse, and its attendant miseries, that people are having to contend with. There is the scary extinction narrative. There is the version in which we are subjugated by a species more intelligent than ourselves. (To understand the consequences of this, think about what we have done to the other species we share our planet with; it makes extinction seem positively attractive.) And then there is the apprehension from the world of non-tech humans – climate-change activists distraught about the carbon footprint of the AI industry; students and workers who see mass unemployment and blank futures; artists, musicians and writers, like myself, who can sense the centrifugal churning that is sucking the beating heart from our bodies and drawing the steel threads of societal control together into one clenched, mechanical fist. How are we supposed to react? By calling for regulations? How do you discipline an industry that makes Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now – racist tropes included – look like a current affairs documentary? Cyclopes is Colonel Kurtz, an ageing ex-marine maddened by the cruelties of war, who rules his unhinged, blood-drenched, drugged-out empire and his native subjects in the Heart of Darkness (transplanted from Conrad’s Africa to Coppola’s Vietnam). The instruction from the US Army high command to the young officer sent to end his fellow marine’s insurrection is unambiguous: “Terminate with extreme prejudice.” What should our slogan be? Regulate with extreme prejudice? Perhaps. Although I honestly don’t know what that means, or looks like. It feels a little like that moment before the tsunami in 2004. Remember how, in Thailand and Indonesia, the ocean drew back from the coastline? People ran out to marvel at the miles of pristine new beach that suddenly emerged, not realising that, far out at sea, a wall of water was building up and would come crashing over them. We’re in that moment now. A towering wall of stupidity is about to inundate us. The trail of delectable crumbs on the shining sand is luring us deeper and deeper into the ocean. It reveals magical treasures, jewelled seashells and secret castles that promise a forever honeymoon, or a moneyhoon, if that’s what you’d prefer. Pick up those shells and marvel at what they can do for you. The ugly name for them is “consumer applications”. They can be your mother, lover, therapist, doctor. They can write novels for you in a minute, in the style of your choosing, and translate them into any language you want. They can edit your films, compose your music, do your research and draft your legal documents. What they can do in the field of medicine is nothing short of a miracle. (It will not stop the poor from continuing to die of cholera, malaria and tuberculosis, or simply of hunger and poverty.) They also promise to deliver instant justice, education and democracy to you via your phone. If you swing the other way, they can improve your Nazi salute and arm you with a mental chainsaw. What’s not to love? How can you resist this? And why should you? For all the talk of AI and authoritarianism, is it not true that some of our best, most beloved antifascist YouTubers and tireless activists (certainly in India), with tens of millions of subscribers collectively, are devoted proponents of AI? Or that the Gen-Z Cockroach uprising against the Modi government, which fell on us like rain on parched earth, rolled in on the most delightful, irreverent AI videos? It is. But when the threat assessment spells real danger, that window can be slammed shut in an instant. As I write this, during what is being called Season 2 of the Cockroach protests in Delhi, the internet in my neighbourhood has been shut down. During other protests in states like Kashmir and Manipur, the Indian government ordered internet shutdowns that lasted for months. Cyclopes is holding up the Machine God, still in his infancy, in its bloodless arms, and inviting us to bow down before him. Trust Him and give Him your everything and, in return, He’ll give you His razzle-dazzle. Colonisation always comes bearing shiny gifts. But AI is colonisation of a kind few of us can even imagine. It’s capitalism’s final destination. Cyclopes is never shy about saying the quiet part out loud. Here, again, is Peter Thiel, chairman of Palantir: “The initial founding vision was that we were going to use technology to change the whole world, to overturn the monetary system of the world… We could never win an election… because we’re in such a small minority. But maybe you could actually unilaterally change the world, without having to constantly convince people and beg people and plead with people who are never going to agree with you.” And here’s Shlomo Kramer, CEO of the Israeli tech company Cato Networks: “It’s time to limit the First Amendment in order to protect it… We need to control the platforms, all the social platforms. We need to stack-rank the authenticity of every person that expresses themselves online and take control over what they are saying, based on that ranking.” This entitlement, this wealth, this power, this presumption, was not given to them by God. It has been seized from us. To train its Machine God, Cyclopes needs to strip-mine and stockpile everything that human civilisation has ever achieved. It wants to mass transfer the cumulative accomplishments, the fruit of the combined labour of millions of us, over thousands of years, including literature, art, music, mathematics, chess, academic research – everything – into company holdings. It will bank this knowledge, find ways of controlling it, sanitising it, politicising it, and deciding who can have access to it and who cannot. And at what price? Let’s call it the privatisation and corporatisation of the history of human endeavour, of civilisation itself. All you need to do is allow your soul to be digitised and turned into data. What remains of you will be human sludge and slurry. Industrial effluent. Here’s Sam Altman again: “We see a future where intelligence is a utility, like electricity or water, and people buy it from us on a meter.”  But is it truly theirs to sell? I am one among hundreds of thousands of authors whose books Anthropic has used without permission to train its LLM. As a result of a class-action suit, I received a notice offering to throw me a couple of thousand dollars per title as a settlement. These are books that took me a lifetime of living, and several years of writing. The notice says that the company downloaded the books from two websites that host pirated PDFs, but “Anthropic denies it did anything wrong”. It offers me a claim number and a pin code. It’s like having the organs of my body harvested without my knowing. Now that the machine has been trained on my work, I fear that very soon, when I write – like myself – in a language that I have laboured for decades to make uniquely mine, I will be told that it doesn’t sound like my work. That it’s actually AI. What shall I do for the rest of my life? Dodge around my own way of writing? Find a new language? What shall we call this? Heart-mining? Brain-mining? Life-mining? In her incisive, dagger-sharp book, Empire of AI, Karen Hao describes the ongoing, all-out plunder of land and resources, and the dragooning of workers in poor countries labouring on starvation wages to become “data capturers” to keep Cyclopes’ dreams afloat. Since there is unlikely to be enough water or electricity to feed the massive energy appetite of its companies and its $100 billion supercomputers, Cyclopes is aggressively lobbying for private nuclear plants and the rollback of safety protocols. As backup, billions of dollars are being poured into developing nonperishable sources of fusion energy, so that data centres can be moved into outer space or onto the moon. Meanwhile, on dear, shabby old Earth, the government of India has stepped up to welcome the setting up of more energy-guzzling data centres. Six in Visakhapatnam alone, including a $15 billion hub for Google. They are being given clearance with virtually zero environmental oversight, as though they’re just buildings, warehouses. It’s an old tradition between India and the US – give us your garbage, your toxic industries, your poisoned chalice. We’ll treasure it. And as in the US, activists in India are putting their bodies on the line to stop the poisoning of the water and the air for the tens of thousands of people who live in the vicinity of the proposed “warehouses”. Anti-data centre activists in the US are being pitted against construction workers who have landed jobs building these massive facilities. These activists, fighting on behalf of local communities, are labelled as foreign-funded traitors, terrorists or left-wing extremists who are stealing jobs from decent, hardworking Americans employed by patriotic US companies. Pitting people against each other like this is a ploy so old that it stinks like a corpse at high noon. Watching it play out in Kerala, the southern state of India where I come from, is how I learned that viewing everything only through the polarising prism of the “left” or the “right” isn’t always useful. Here’s a little story, far removed in both space and time, but one that still holds lessons for the present. One of the first things that Kerala’s first democratically elected Communist government did in the late 1950s was to invite a big corporation to set up a rayon factory in the north of the state, upstream from the city of Calicut on the banks of the Chaliyar River. The industrialist promised that the factory would create 3,000 jobs, asking in return for government subsidies on raw materials, electricity and water. It was given bamboo from the forests nearby at one rupee per tonne, while bamboo workers, mostly indigenous people, had to buy it at one rupee for a single culm. When the factory started production, it took in more water in one day than all of Calicut city, then dumped its poisonous effluent straight back into the river. Downstream, the city water was polluted. Fish died. Thousands of fishermen lost their livelihoods. When all the available bamboo had been consumed, they started using eucalyptus. Acres of dense, old-growth forest were clear-felled for a monoculture eucalyptus plantation. Thousands of forest dwellers, bamboo and wicker workers lost their livelihoods. But the 3,000 factory workers unionised themselves, and thrived. Until, over time, poisonous factory fumes began to cause outbreaks of cancer and respiratory illness among the workers. They went on strike demanding compensation. The industrialist built a (private) cancer hospital. The militant factory workers held sit-ins and lockouts demanding pay hikes and other benefits. They won small, incremental victories for themselves, and went back to work.  After a few years, the eucalyptus plantation vanished, too. The factory closed down. The workers with good union jobs went on hunger strike demanding it be reopened. It never was.  This is a dilemma – almost an existential challenge – for the “data capturer” labour force around the world too. India, with its massive population, is a data feast for Cyclopes’ insatiable appetite. The poorest of the poor, who live in outlying villages and small towns, are being conscripted to supply every conceivable kind of information that can be mined. Workers on construction sites and factory floors are required to work with cameras fixed to their heads so that AI can cannibalise their movements to train the robots that will soon replace them. The workers know they are digging their own graves, but they can’t refuse, because multitudes are waiting to take their place. Once their jobs are gone, what will the world do with the millions of “surplus people”, the fascist classification for those who consume the Earth’s limited resources but do not contribute to society? Fascists have long had their own genocidal ideas about this. Cyclopes – or the Nerd Reich, as Gil Durán calls it in his book of that title – has at times flirted with another path. It toys in an on-again, off-again way with the idea of a Universal Basic Income (UBI). With other people’s money. Not its own. How cool and anticapitalist is that? Perhaps it should try supporting itself on a monthly UBI payment for a couple of years. Perhaps that should be step one in the Regulate with Extreme Prejudice programme. Let’s state this for the record: everybody in the world could receive a Universal Basic Income today, right now, if wealth were more evenly distributed. You don’t need to destroy the planet to do that. And by the way, who is going to disburse the UBI? Who will decide who is eligible and who is not? Just asking. Perhaps, elaborating on Comrade Shlomo Kramer’s theme, people can be stack-ranked according to their race, caste, religion, gender, political views and obedience quotients? Or perhaps the Indian government can lend a hand. In its recently conducted Special Intensive Revision of the country’s voter rolls, 130 million people have been deleted. Almost a tenth of the population. A nice big chunk. A civilised form of culling. They wouldn’t be eligible for a UBI, or for any rights at all. In states like Assam, some of them are employed as construction labourers to build the huge detention centres meant to house people like themselves. A government elects its people. Cyclopes controls the government. Neat. Then there’s the well-intentioned democratic socialist version. Bernie Sanders wants the public – the North American public, at any rate – to have direct ownership of the AI companies. He suggests a one-off 50% tax on the biggest AI companies’ stock, to create a sovereign wealth fund with independent oversight. This fund would apparently be worth nearly $7 trillion, from which hundreds of billions of dollars would be paid every year directly to US citizens, as well as to health care, housing and education programmes. (Again, the trillions already exist. The political will does not. What would change?) But even in this democratic socialist option, data will still be sucked out of the South – India, Africa, South America – while the profits stay in the North. Of course, companies should pay for data. But has it already come to this? Is getting shares in the apocalypse our only option now? While there is so much debate about what AI can and cannot do for humans, there is too little talk about what it’s doing to humans. Studies have warned of a relationship between AI and cognitive decline in human beings. Human intelligence looks set to plunge in proportion with the rise of artificial intelligence. Perhaps our unused brains will atrophy, our heads will shrink and our fingers will turn into undulating prompt tentacles. Those of us who have already lived our lives in a different kind of world know what we are losing. But what of the generation that is about to come of age? Will it have its own language, its own thoughts, its own grief? Will it have the right to strive? To fall? To fail? To be imperfect? Will it experience the impossible pain and ecstatic pleasure of solving a math equation or creating art or literature or music of its own – however flawed? The triumph of AI will be a crime against humanness. It will bottle our brains in formaldehyde. It will destroy the world as we know it. The men who promote it and profit from it are cognisant of this, and have already made arrangements to exit into another realm. The oligarchs are announcing the battle lines loudly, proudly: that it is us against them. They suggest, without flinching, that for Cyclopes to thrive, humanity may have to die. The young generation that is rising up to fight it understands this. I know that, earlier in this essay, I suggested we should “regulate with extreme prejudice”. But what I really want to say about those AI companies is this: terminate with extreme prejudice. Part of this essay will be delivered as a lecture at The People’s AI Assembly on 19 October in New York City.
