... Two fourth-quarter throws helped end Texas' perfect season last Saturday against Oklahoma. They also raised questions about the most famous QB prospect in college football. First came Arch Manning's pick-6 with 10:07 remaining, giving Oklahoma the lead. Then, after Texas tied it, Manning's second pick in the final 30 seconds set up the Sooners' game-winning field goal in a 27-24 shocker. Manning had some brilliant moments in the first three quarters of the Red River Rivalry, including two high-level touchdown throws, and he added another terrific TD pass between the two interceptions. But the two turnovers proved decisive in the loss.  It was a near-perfect encapsulation of Arch, the NFL prospect: brilliant mixed with maddening. "Bad decision, bad mechanics, bad throw," an AFC scouting director said of the pick-6. "But he did some good things in that game. Really good. That's where you're kind of stuck as an evaluator. Like, how do I judge this?" Two bad throws from Arch Manning upended Texas in its rivalry game against Oklahoma and reshaped NFL Draft discussions about the QB. Blessed with NFL-caliber skills and QB-royalty bloodlines, Manning entered this season as the presumptive top QB prospect in what has been touted as a potentially great 2027 NFL Draft class at the position. But an uneven start to his 2026 season has NFL talent evaluators questioning what they're seeing — and whether Manning has made the kind of progress expected from a provisional No. 1 overall draft pick. Two evaluators we spoke to were ambivalent about Manning as a prospect right now. Both see some of the same symptoms — late reads, not enough on-time throws, poor ball placement — and agree that the product has been slightly disappointing to this point, even if hope in Manning remains relatively high.  "He's athletic. He has the tools, but it's still coming together," one senior NFC evaluator said. "... Right now he's not ready, just as a complete prospect, of reading coverages, making good decisions and delivering accurate balls on a consistent basis. It's just not there. ... It's coming. You see the glimpses. He's tough. He's competitive. He uses his legs." The quarterback hierarchy for the 2027 draft is far from set in stone. But Manning's perceived grip on the top spot has significantly loosened, especially as, on balance, Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker, Ole Miss' Trinidad Chambliss and Miami's Darian Mensah have authored arguably more impressive tape this season and prospects such as Notre Dame's CJ Carr and Missouri's Austin Simmons have made big moves from the start of the season. "I think we tend to rush [Manning's] development just because of his last name," the NFC evaluator said. "... I don't think it's there yet. There's a lot more polished guys that are farther along than he is." Can Manning reestablish his draft standing with a strong finish like he had in 2025? Are his mistakes fixable? And could he even return to college next season? All those questions hang in the air as Manning and Texas enter a crucial stage of their season. Manning, the grandson of former Saints legend Archie Manning and the nephew of Peyton and Eli Manning, had greatness projected on him before he ever set foot in Texas. But after nearly four years of college, starting for the past two seasons, his picture remains incomplete.  This was supposed to be Manning's breakthrough season. The surge began in the second half of the 2025 season, when he played some of the best ball of his college career. In Texas' final six games, Manning threw for 1,714 yards, 14 TDs and two interceptions, ran for 206 yards and five more scores and even caught a TD pass.  Texas added wideout Cam Coleman, offensive tackle Melvin Siani and running backs Raleek Brown and Hollywood Smothers, and retained a host of blue-chip talent, including future first-rounders such as OT Trevor Goosby and WR Ryan Wingo. Even in the rough-and-tumble SEC, with Texas facing arguably the nation's toughest schedule, greatness was the expectation. That hasn't quite happened yet. Manning and Texas have yet to reach their peaks, even with a shocking 20-point comeback over then-No. 1 Ohio State in Week 2. In that game, Manning pulled off the stunner with three TD drives in the fourth quarter. Even that outing came with its warts. "I didn't think he was that good [against OSU]," the AFC director said. "He helped them win for sure, but he had plays to make that he just flat-out missed. They were very lucky to win that one." Three up-and-down games later, including the fourth-quarter mistakes against Oklahoma, Manning feels like he's in the same place he was before the hot finish last season. The high-end throws are highly enticing. The critical errors are a serious deterrent. Manning remains a complicated prospect. Then again, several flawed prospects have ended up being drafted very high in recent years. Blake Bortles (2014, No. 3), Josh Allen (2018, No. 7), Daniel Jones (2019, No. 6) and Zach Wilson (2021, No. 2) are examples of prospects who, regardless of how their NFL careers have turned out, landed in the top 10 while facing questions about accuracy, mechanics and decision-making.  In a traits-over-production league, there are still enough positive elements to Manning's game that could keep him close to the top of the draft. There is also the desperation factor. "Every year there's more quarterback-needy teams than there are early [QB prospects]," the NFC evaluator said. "That's where you get the fourth guy [in Round 1], you know? Where he's really the sixth or seventh guy, but he's the fourth guy for this year. ...  "We sometimes grasp for salvation at that position." Neither evaluator was willing to reveal exactly where they'd slot Manning in this class given how relatively early it is in the draft process.  "You don't always have the answers," the senior NFC talent evaluator said. "Middle of October, you're finding out what it is and what are the questions that need to be asked." An echo of his play in the back half of 2025 could vault Manning back up toward the top of the class. But what if his season continues on the current trajectory or slides even further down? "I can see the kid coming back," the NFC evaluator said. "You know, you're talking about wise counsel [in the Manning family]. I think he's going to make a good decision regardless. … It'll be interesting." One NFL scout Yahoo Sports spoke with compared Arch Manning to the Colts' Daniel Jones, pictured here in 2026. Because of his pedigree and impressive physical qualities, most Manning comps start with big names. Yet the scouting director found a more apples-to-apples comparison farther down the food chain. Josh Allen? "No." Trevor Lawrence? "Trevor was more polished," the AFC director said. Drake Maye? "Closer, but not exactly who I thought." Who then? "I see Daniel Jones. Daniel Jones is a pretty good quarterback, now. Arch is, too. But style-wise, and just the questions that come into my head when I watch him, it's like the Daniel Jones experience all over again: big, talented, athletic kid … decision-making questionable, [inconsistent] ball placement. That's what I've seen so far." Both evaluators agree that getting to the root of Manning's unsteadiness is the key to unlocking him as a prospect. "It's not only tape; it's going through and getting an understanding of the whys behind it," the NFC evaluator said. "... That's part of the deep dive." The biggest word that comes up with Manning? Consistency. "More tools-traits prospect than complete player, to me, right now," the AFC director said. "He's at, what, 20 or so starts? But it's been four years in the same system. … You'd like to see more development by this stage." The director has attended one of Manning's games in person this season and seen most of the tape from his five games. Even while noting that Texas' issues are far from all being on Manning, there have still been too many issues cropping up on his tape — even on successful plays. "It just looks like he's not seeing the field that great," the AFC director added. "Extra hitches when they're not needed. Getting hung up on [his first reads]. Turning down open throws. Late on some stuff, even completions. Ball placement, not always great. Sacks that shouldn't be sacks. … He's leaving some meat on that bone, and I'd like to see it picked cleaner." The other issue seems to be game feel: knowing when to press and when to be smart. That was on display in the Oklahoma loss, but it's also shown up in other games. "It's him risk-taking when you want the checkdown, and it's a checkdown when you want him taking chances," the director said. "It's backward to me. I'd like to know what he's thinking on some of these throws, or what he's been taught. Because some of it doesn't make sense." Manning has seven games left in the regular season, with his draft stock and Texas' season hanging in the balance. The Longhorns' next three games are in Austin, starting with a Florida team that flummoxed Manning in 2025, followed by tough home games against No. 9 Ole Miss and No. 16 Mississippi State. After a couple more difficult road games at No. 13 Missouri and No. 22 LSU, Texas finishes at home with current SEC bottom dwellers Arkansas and Texas A&M.  This stretch will determine whether Manning and Texas can fulfill their lofty expectations. Both evaluators agree that the potential is there for both quarterback and team to finish on high notes. The talent is there. The bulk of the season remains in front of them. But one way or another, for Manning to reach his ceiling, he's going to have to beat the clock — both in the pocket and in his head. "We just gotta play more on time, man," the AFC director said.

Victor Miller, who wrote the screenplay for the original Friday the 13th, died on August 31, 2026, in Alameda, California. He was 86. Miller was born in New Orleans in 1940, was paid $9,282 for the script in 1979, and was never shy about what he thought was wrong with every Friday the 13th movie that came after his. The cleanest version of his complaint sat in an FAQ on his own website, online by 2011 at the latest: âTo be honest, I have not seen any of the sequels, but I have a major problem with all of them because they made Jason the villain.â  âJason was dead from the very beginning. He was a victim, not a villain,â the writer added, calling a mother as the killer âthe best part of my screenplay.â In Millerâs script, the murderer is Pamela Voorhees, a mother killing camp counselors to avenge the death of her young son, and Jason exists only as her motive. Bring him back as the killer and the motive goes with him.  âOnly because it completely destroys the motivation for Mrs. Voorhees!â Miller laughed as he told Vice in 2015 when asked about his website entry. âWhich was the only thing I had going for me in that movie, which was that she was avenging her son and then it turns out that he isnât dead anyway.â  Two years earlier he had put it more bluntly to the site Trainwreckâd Society: bringing Jason back âmay have been a revenue stream, but it eviscerated Mrs. Voorheesâ raison dâ murder.â To the fan site Friday the 13th: The Website, he called Jason âjust a stock villainâ and added, âI donât have much sympathy for him.â He didnât even get the last word on his own ending. In a sworn declaration quoted by a federal appeals court in 2021, Friday the 13th director Sean S. Cunningham said financier Phil Scuderi proposed the shock in which Jason comes out of the lake, that Jason ânever appears in any of Millerâs drafts,â and that Miller âwas vehemently opposed to the idea of Jason coming back to life at all.â  Miller told the fan site a different story: he wrote Jason popping out of the water himself, âusing pretty much the Carrie ending shot-for-shot,â and drove the pages over to Cunninghamâs production office separately. âThatâs why the pages never appeared in my own draft.â The story wasnât his only grievance. When Vice asked whether his objection was purely about continuity, Miller said, âWell, that and that I wasnât invited to participate in the sequels,â adding, âThe two put together make the whole.â  He said heâd been told he was too expensive for Part 2, explaining, âSequels have to be made cheaper than the previous one. And I went, âOh. OK.â What did I know? Iâd never written a hit movie before.â He doubted it would have mattered anyway: âI probably would have fought the idea of making Jason the bad guy and been fired from the project anyway,â he told the fan site. Miller kept getting paid either way. As he told Vice, âevery time they make a new [Friday the 13th movie], I get a little check,â and the court record puts a number on part of it: a Writers Guild settlement of $27,396.46 in the late 1980s over unpaid sequel and residual payments. What Miller loved was the villain he actually wrote. He told Trainwreckâd Society that he had made âa mother become a super-villain, breaking the boundaries of horror,â and gotten âa fantasy mom who would kill to punish anyone who was mean to her kid.â  Millerâs own mother, he added, might have said something else if he had drowned: âI told you not to go near the water. Tokenized stocks are drawing trading activity beyond Wall Street hours, while Bitcoin miners confront costly AI expansion and new accounting rules could benefit stablecoins. Tokenization is beginning to reshape traditional financial markets, with stocks increasingly in focus. Much of the attention has centered on the $3.3 billion in tokenized equities now onchain, according to RWA.xyz, but one of the biggest innovations may be what happens before Wall Street opens and after it closes. According to the latest industry data, more than 70% of tokenized stock trading volume on BNB Chain now occurs outside regular US market hours, with similar patterns emerging on Solana and Base. Tokenized equities allow investors to trade US stocks across time zones without waiting for Wall Street’s opening bell, potentially changing how liquidity is distributed throughout the day. However, many platforms driving this activity remain off-limits to American investors, even as US regulators begin to make room for tokenized stock trading. This week’s Crypto Biz looks at tokenized stock trading, the economics of Bitcoin mining, proposed accounting rules that could make it easier for companies to treat stablecoins as cash equivalents, and Strive’s expanding Bitcoin treasury. Most tokenized stock trading on Solana and BNB Chain now takes place outside regular US market hours, suggesting that around-the-clock access is becoming a major selling point for equities issued onchain. According to Blockworks data cited by The Kobeissi Letter, more than 70% of tokenized stock trading volume on BNB Chain occurs outside the traditional 9:30 am to 4:00 pm Eastern trading window. The figure is 63% on Solana and nearly 60% on Base. Activity is also picking up. Jupiter reported a 50% month-over-month increase in tokenized asset trading volume, while RWA.xyz data showed the value of tokenized stocks climbing 15% over the past 30 days to nearly $3.3 billion. The trend comes as the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s innovation exemption opens the door for qualifying platforms to trade tokenized US-listed stocks on public blockchains, subject to disclosure and shareholder protection requirements. However, existing offerings such as xStocks and Ondo Global Markets remain largely unavailable to US investors, limiting domestic participation in the growing market. A proposed change to US accounting standards could make stablecoins more attractive to corporate treasuries by allowing qualifying tokens to be treated as cash equivalents on company balance sheets, according to a report from payments blockchain Tempo. Under current accounting practices, stablecoin holdings may not count toward a company’s reported cash reserves, potentially affecting liquidity ratios and loan covenants even when the tokens are fully backed by US dollars. The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) proposal could change that, though Tempo noted that companies would need direct redemption rights with stablecoin issuers to qualify. For example, simply purchasing USDC through a cryptocurrency exchange would not necessarily meet that requirement. Coinbase already classified USDC and other payment stablecoins as cash equivalents in its 2025 annual report, supported by its redemption arrangement with Circle. The proposal is open for public comment until Nov. 19, after which FASB will review the feedback before determining the final rules and their effective date. Holding is widely touted as a great way to build wealth in the crypto market, but it hasn't worked for every coin. Take XRP (XRP), the payments-focused cryptocurrency native to the XRP Ledger and the world’s fifth-largest digital asset by market value. The token is still trading well below its 2017 cycle high, while most other major cryptocurrencies have climbed far above theirs. In 2017, crypto broke into the mainstream, pulling in new users and investors during the frenzied run that carried into the first week or two of 2018. XRP currently trades around $1.33, down 62.5% from its early January 2018 peak of $3.55. In other words, an XRP buyer from that peak is still underwater nearly nine years later. (XRP did briefly top its old high, reaching $3.66 in July 2025 before crashing.) Bitcoin BTC$81,353.01 is up 314% from its December 2017 peak of $19,804. Dogecoin DOGE$0.08007 is up 322% from its January 2018 high, and BNB BNB$719.90 is up about 2,800%. Ether ETH$2,417.56 is up 66% and zcash (ZEC) is up 38%. Tron is also slightly below its peak, down about 4%. Solana launched in 2020. Bitcoin, ether and many other tokens have pulled back sharply from their 2025 peaks, yet remain far above their 2017 highs. Analysts point first to XRP’s supply. "Circulating supply grew 63%, from 38.7B in 2017 to 63.1B, while XRP's total market value fell only about 3%," Nicolai Sondergaard, senior research analyst at analytics firm Nansen, told CoinDesk. "More XRP in circulation means each token represents a smaller share of roughly the same total value." Circulating supply is the number of coins on the market, and as it grows, each coin represents a smaller share of the total.  Oliver Carding, head of marketing at Tesseract Group, says XRP looks better when measured by total value instead of price. "On value, XRP recovered," he said. "About 63% more XRP is in circulation than at that peak, so the same circulating market capitalization would mean a price roughly 39% lower." Tesseract is an institutional digital asset management firm that manages over $500 million in assets under management. U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds, or ETFs, have opened the door for institutional investors to take exposure to digital assets. While bitcoin and ether funds have pulled in billions, XRP funds have lagged big time. "ETF uptake has also been muted relative to $BTC and $ETH," said Paul Howard, senior director at market-making firm Wincent. To date, XRP funds have pulled in just $1.80 billion in investor money since debuting nearly a year ago, according to data source SoSoValue. Bitcoin ETFs often attract over $1 billion in investor money in a single day. Nansen's data also shows trading activity has weakened, with XRP spot volume down 53.5%, perpetual futures volume down 44%, and active addresses down 10.7%. Ripple, the payments company closely tied to XRP, has focused on cross-border payments rather than chasing sectors such as DeFi, AI, and memecoins, which have attracted greater capital flows and deeper integration with traditional finance. "Ripple, meanwhile, has been working hard to build payment infrastructure, RLUSD and trade financing products around the usage of the ledger and coin, and this has taken focus from just core XRP," Howard said. Investors also have more choices now. "The role of DeFi for investment into ETH, SOL and HYPE has also been a new narrative which $XRP has not focused on," Howard said. Ripple’s legal fight with U.S. regulators also held XRP back. The Securities and Exchange Commission sued Ripple and two of its executives in December 2020, saying the company had raised about $1.3 billion by selling XRP without registering it as a security. A federal judge ruled in 2023 that XRP sales on public exchanges were not securities offerings, but that sales to institutional investors were. In 2024, Ripple was ordered to pay a $125 million penalty. The case ended in August 2025, when both sides dropped their appeals. Carding said the prolonged regulatory uncertainty helps explain why the token missed its old high during the 2021 crypto bull run, when Coinbase suspended trading. “The SEC case helps explain why XRP did not revisit its 2018 high in 2021, when Coinbase suspended trading, but the appeals were dropped in August 2025 with XRP above $3,” Carding said. “Since then, XRP is down about 59%, against 32% for bitcoin and 44% for ether, and its circulating market capitalisation is down about 56%.” XRP isn't the only coin trading below its early 2018 highs. "On price, six of the other nine assets in the January 2018 top ten are further below their levels of that week," Carding said. For those watching XRP, Carding has a suggestion. "What I would watch is XRP against bitcoin, alongside net monthly distribution after re-escrow and changes in fund holdings," he said. "Relative weakness that persists as distribution slows would point to weaker demand." In plain English, Carding is watching whether XRP underperforms bitcoin even as fewer new XRP tokens enter the market through Ripple’s escrow releases. If supply growth slows but XRP still lags bitcoin, it would suggest that investor demand for XRP is weakening. SSD prices are bad right now. Storage drive prices rose alongside memory and other hardware during the AI boom, and they show no sign of coming down anytime soon. If 2026 is anything to go by, anyone requiring new storage is going to be forking out some serious cash in 2027 and beyond. But what if there was another way? Storage prices aren't the only problem with the hardware shortages. In some cases, developers can be held responsible for putting additional pressure on our storage drives, with enormous game files requiring hundreds of gigabytes — only to reverse the requirements in some cases. So, before you reach deep into your already overstretched pockets to add more capacity, find out how much of what's on your system perhaps doesn't need to be there. Owning a massive drive is bliss after years of fretting about storage for years.  We know that SSDs are expensive. Storage is at a premium everywhere you look, so it's interesting that some developers are taking stock of their creations and realizing they might not need as much space. 2024 smash-hit Helldivers 2 is a prime example. The game originally launched with an installation size of roughly 154GB, putting it right up there among the biggest PC games by file size, as per GameRant. By the end of 2025, Arrowhead managed to reduce the Helldivers 2 Steam installation by 85%, cutting it from 154GB to just 23GB. If you had Helldivers 2 (154GB), God of War Ragnarok (190GB), Medal of Honor: Above and Beyond (180GB), Starfield (150GB), Red Dead Redemption 2 (150GB), and Baldur's Gate 3 (150GB) installed on one drive, that's the best part of a terabyte on six games. Six incredible games that will keep you entertained for years, in fairness, but still, it's a lot. Writing on Steam, Arrowhead said that the company made the reductions by "completely de-duplicating our data," essentially optimizing its data files by removing the duplicate files primarily designed to speed boot times on older hard drives. With just 11 percent of Helldivers 2 players using hard drives, it meant the other 89 percent of players were suffering this enormous installation size. The reduction caused minimal impact on HDD mission load times, and everyone gets back a huge chunk of storage. Helldivers 2 isn't the only game in recent years to give back some storage. The August 2026 Marvel Rivals Season 9.5 Update delivered a texture compression overhaul that dropped the installation size by 40GB on PC. Similarly, Sea of Thieves is receiving a second size-saving pass from developer Rare that should reduce its install size by 50%, dropping from around 130GB to 65GB or so, and a few years back Fortnite managed to slash its install size from 90GB to 35GB with some file restructuring and compression.  In many cases, it feels like developers are just lazy, but that's typically far from the case; it's tempting, but wrong. There are clear reasons why these space-munching trade-offs are made, and why in some cases, they're reversed. Helldivers 2 is the perfect example, again. Duplicating assets spares a mechanical drive from hunting across the disk, so Arrowhead built the PC version around that. The problem was the premise: the industry load-time figures it relied on turned out to be wrong, and most of the game's loading time comes from level generation rather than asset loading. Swapping it around cut the bloat. Other major storage handbacks have come from developers changing how their game operates. Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 launched with a whopping installation size of 310GB, but that instantly dropped to 90GB if you removed the bundled Modern Warfare assets — but that wasn't made clear to most users, who had to find the full disk space. If you just wanted the BO6 campaign and multiplayer, it was just 56GB or so. So, not a case of Treyarch and Raven colluding to force you to buy more storage, although it felt like it. It was just a case of really poor communication, whipped up by some media hysteria about enormous installations. The biggest problem is that for every Helldivers 2 that takes the time to work with a team to reduce its file size, there's an Ark Survival demanding hundreds of gigabytes either way, so the payoff for your storage capacity feels futile.  There are a few options for those moments when you need space in a hurry. Everyone has games they've meant to play installed, and removing those is a sure-fire way to grab some much-needed storage back during these times of need. My own Steam list pictured above is a prime example; I'm not much of a gamer these days, yet I have heaps of games installed at all times! In November 2025, TweakTown reported that leading SSD controller manufacturer Phison said all storage makers had already sold out of 2026 capacity, a message echoed by other manufacturers. It's a similar story for 2027, with Samsung, SanDisk, Micron, and other NAND flash (and DRAM) manufacturers largely selling out their capacity for the next 12 months and more. That means one thing: higher storage prices will continue until morale improves. Given the AI boom shows no sign of slowing down, the cheapest time to buy storage is likely now, because it's highly unlikely to change next year. Is that the tinkling of Santa's sleigh I hear in the very far distance? Or the massed mobs of Black Friday deal-hunters queuing before dawn? Your smart home can be set up to do so many things. It can turn on lights when no one is home. It can keep an eye on different areas of your home with smart cameras. Plus, you can automate all kinds of devices to work without you needing to touch them. As stated, you don't have to be home to have your smart devices work. The brilliance of smart devices is that many of them can tell you where people are nearby. For security purposes, smart home devices are some of the best options on the market. Motion sensors are some of the most popular options when it comes to setting up your home with smart home security devices. But if you don't want your phone pinging every few minutes when someone walks by one, you can still understand whether there's motion in your home with other devices. This easy to install device alerts me as soon as my mail arrives.  I'm a big fan of Kasa Smart Wi-Fi Plugs because they are easy to use within pretty much any smart home ecosystem. Whether you have Samsung SmartThings, Amazon Alexa, Apple HomeKit, or you rely on a Home Assistant, you can utilize these smart plugs. Smart plugs can be controlled with ease, either via app or via voice controls. Setting up automations and allowing them to control your devices that are plugged into them makes your life simpler. What I love about these smart plugs is that they actually provide energy monitoring for the devices that are plugged into them. You can get a full report of what the device has been up to, helping you manage your electricity bill. This also gives you a good idea as to what rooms of the house people are spending the most time in, helping you get a full breakdown of what's happening with your devices. Discovery with $606 million in his pockets following its merger into the larger Skydance empire, an extraordinary payday for an executive whose four-year tenure was defined by layoffs, cost-cutting, canceled projects, removed content, and a relentless effort to reduce the debt created by the merger that put him in charge. The payout, disclosed in a securities filing last week, comes as the newly combined media empire prepares for another round of restructuring, having already warned employees of “difficult decisions that affect our workforce.” According to Variety, Zaslav received $606.1 million in stock-related compensation following the October 6 completion of the Paramount-WBD merger, including roughly $381.7 million in stock options. The figure is distinct from earlier golden-parachute estimates that included potential severance and other benefits. The payout scale is particularly striking, given that WBD shareholders had already rejected the executive compensation arrangements in a nonbinding vote. In April, 82% of shareholders, four out of every five, voted against the merger-related compensation packages. The board proceeded anyway. And this follows years of eye-watering compensation for Zaslav while thousands of employees lost their livelihoods or had their work canceled or vaulted away. His 2025 compensation alone reached $165 million, including nearly $110 million in stock options awarded for a proposed corporate breakup that never happened. For Warner Bros.’ rank and file, that must be a difficult pill to swallow. Under Zaslav, WBD eliminated jobs across television, streaming, animation, and corporate divisions. The company also became notorious for shelving completed or nearly completed films, including Batgirl, Scoob! Holiday Haunt, and Coyote vs. Acme, turning the studio into a symbol of Hollywood’s longstanding shift away from art and toward commerce. Even judged strictly on financial performance, Zaslav’s tenure was, at best, a mixed bag. WBD reduced gross debt from approximately $53 billion in 2022 to $33.1 billion by June 2026, but fell well short of its original earnings projections. Zaslav initially promised $14 billion in annual adjusted EBITDA by 2023; WBD generated approximately $8.7 billion in 2025. Streaming eventually exceeded expectations, and the Paramount acquisition delivered a premium to shareholders, but neither erases years of disappointing results, and neither will likely console people who have dedicated their careers to those ends and now face an uncertain future. Meanwhile, the benefits of restructuring were distributed very differently from its costs. Zaslav and four other senior WBD executives collected a combined $1.1 billion in stock-related compensation from the merger, according to TheWrap. Arguing that those rewards were commensurate with their performance would require a remarkably generous interpretation of the company’s record. And that’s without considering its responsibilities to its workers and the art they create. And the layoffs aren’t over. The newly combined company, $80 billion in debt, is targeting at least $6 billion in annual cost savings within three years. In a memo to employees, CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz forecasted those “difficult decisions” to signal further cuts. Management says most savings will come from areas other than labor, but it expects additional job losses, with no indication yet of how many positions will be made redundant. Zaslav, meanwhile, exits with a windfall that would take someone earning $100,000 annually more than 6,000 years to accumulate. It aptly illustrates the economics of modern Hollywood, where executives can be rewarded spectacularly for restructuring struggling companies, selling assets, and delivering shareholder returns, while the workers who created those assets are left to absorb the fallout. Warner Bros. Discovery’s employees helped deliver the debt reduction for which Zaslav is being rewarded. Many are now waiting to find out whether they still have jobs.
